column1: This large-scale integrative experiment systematically varied 14 public goods game parameters across 360 unique conditions to assess the effect of punishment on group efficiency. While punishment consistently increased contributions, its effect on efficiency (group payoff relative to full cooperation) was highly heterogeneous: in some settings, punishment increased efficiency, but in many others, it reduced it, often substantially. The direction and magnitude of punishment's effect on efficiency depended on complex interactions between game design features, with communication, contribution framing, contribution type, game length, peer outcome visibility, and reward availability emerging as key moderators.

Punishment in public goods games robustly increases contributions but has a highly variable effect on efficiency, ranging from strongly positive to strongly negative depending on the game context. On average, punishment reduced normalized efficiency, but this average masked substantial heterogeneity: in some parameter settings, punishment improved group welfare, while in others it led to large efficiency losses. The most important predictors of punishment's effect on efficiency were the availability of communication (chat), contribution framing (opt-in vs. opt-out), contribution type (variable vs. all-or-nothing), game length (number of rounds), peer outcome visibility, and the presence of a reward mechanism. These features often interacted, such that, for example, longer games only increased punishment effectiveness when communication was available. Predictive models using these parameters and control efficiency outperformed both laypeople and domain experts in forecasting the effect of punishment on efficiency in new settings.

This paper provides direct, high-quality evidence for predicting the effect of punishment on efficiency in public goods games as a function of game design dimensions and control efficiency. It demonstrates that the effect of punishment is not uniform but depends on complex, sometimes non-intuitive interactions among design features. The most predictive dimensions for efficiency outcomes are communication, contribution framing, contribution type, game length, peer outcome visibility, and reward availability. The paper's dataset and predictive models can be used to estimate treatment efficiency in new PGG designs, and the findings caution against assuming that punishment will always improve welfare, even when it increases cooperation. For prediction tasks, the paper supports using machine learning models trained on these dimensions and control efficiency, rather than relying on expert intuition or simple heuristics.

column1: In a lab public goods game with heterogeneous MPCRs (one high-benefit member, two low-benefit members), the introduction of punishment opportunities does not significantly increase group efficiency or average earnings compared to the control (no incentives) condition. In contrast, reward opportunities substantially increase both contributions and efficiency. Punishment is not effective in this heterogeneous setting, and may even be counterproductive due to antisocial punishment by high-benefit members.

The paper finds that in public goods games with heterogeneous groups (MPCRs 0.9 and 0.4), allowing punishment does not significantly increase group efficiency or average earnings compared to the control (no incentives) condition. Average per-period earnings in the punishment condition (17.007 tokens) are actually lower than in the control (23.860 tokens), and after adjusting for the resource destruction effect of punishment, final earnings in the punishment condition (23.630 tokens) are still not higher than control. In contrast, reward opportunities lead to much higher efficiency and earnings. The lack of effectiveness of punishment is attributed to antisocial punishment by high-benefit members and lack of strategic punishment by low-benefit members. The results are robust across group and individual analyses, and the paper provides direct evidence that punishment does not improve efficiency in this heterogeneous PGG setting.

This paper provides strong evidence that, in public goods games with heterogeneous MPCRs, enabling punishment does not improve efficiency relative to the control (no-punishment) condition. For prediction tasks, if the game design matches this paper (3 players, MPCRs 0.9/0.4, no chat, continuous contributions, punishment cost 1:3, no rewards in punishment condition, 10 rounds, full feedback), the expected efficiency with punishment enabled should be similar to or lower than the control efficiency. The paper also shows that reward is much more effective than punishment in this context. The findings are directly relevant for predicting the effect of punishment on efficiency in heterogeneous PGGs.

column1: This laboratory experiment uses a standard public good game with a leader who can punish at a cost, and manipulates the framing of the leader's role (authority vs. responsibility) and the method of leader selection (willingness to lead vs. voting). The main finding is that when the leader's role is framed as responsibility and leaders are selected by voting, group efficiency (measured by group income) is significantly higher in female-led groups than in male-led groups or in authority-framed conditions. The effect is driven by higher leader contributions and, to a lesser extent, more targeted punishment. In other conditions, the framing effect is weaker or absent. The study provides direct evidence that punishment-enabled leadership can increase efficiency, especially when combined with responsibility framing and female leaders.

The experiment finds that introducing a leader with the power to punish increases group contributions and efficiency compared to the no-leader baseline. When the leader's role is framed as responsibility (rather than authority), and especially when the leader is selected by voting, female leaders are more effective at increasing group income and efficiency than male leaders. The responsibility framing increases both leader contributions and the effectiveness of punishment, but the positive effect on efficiency is robustly observed only in the voting stage for female-led groups. In other conditions (authority framing, male leaders, or self-selected leaders), the efficiency gains from punishment are smaller or not significant. The study also shows that leader contributions are a more important driver of efficiency than punishment per se, as punishment can offset its own benefits through costs. Overall, the presence of punishment increases efficiency, but the magnitude depends on leader gender, framing, and selection method.

This paper provides strong evidence that enabling punishment in a public good game increases efficiency, especially when the leader is female, the leadership role is framed as responsibility, and the leader is selected by voting. The game design dimensions most relevant for predicting efficiency gains from punishment are: presence of a leader with punishment power, punishment cost and effectiveness, group size (4), number of rounds (5), and information structure (no chat, summary feedback). The control (no-leader) efficiency is reported, and the treatment (punishment-enabled) efficiency is higher, particularly in the responsibility/voting/female leader condition. For prediction, the paper suggests that punishment is most effective at increasing efficiency when the leader is prosocial (as selected or induced by responsibility framing), and that leader contributions are a key mechanism. The results are directly relevant for predicting efficiency in similar lab PGGs with punishment, especially with comparable group size, round number, and punishment parameters.

column1: The paper finds that making punishment redistributive (so that fines are transferred to other group members as rewards) increases both contributions and efficiency in a voluntary contribution mechanism (VCM) public goods game. Even after netting out the direct resource effect of redistribution, efficiency is higher in the redistributive punishment treatment than in standard punishment. Redistributive punishment also reduces perverse punishment (punishment of high contributors) and makes it more profitable to contribute, as the return to contribution becomes positive.

In a repeated public goods game with four players and 20 rounds, the authors compare standard costly punishment (where fines are burned) to a redistributive punishment treatment (where fines are transferred to other group members as rewards). Both treatments use the same marginal per capita return (MPCR = 0.4), punishment cost (0.25 per unit), and group structure. The redistributive punishment treatment leads to significantly higher average contributions (9.03 vs. 7.09), higher average earnings (15.18 vs. 12.88), and higher efficiency, even after controlling for the resource-conserving effect of redistribution (earnings net of transfers: 14.20 vs. 12.88). The effect on efficiency is marginally statistically significant after netting out transfers. Redistributive punishment also reduces the share of punishment targeted at high contributors and increases the monetary return to contributing (from negative to positive). The study provides direct evidence that the design of the punishment mechanism can moderate the efficiency impact of punishment in public goods games.

This paper provides strong evidence that, in a standard linear public goods game with four players, 20 rounds, no communication, and fixed partners, enabling punishment increases contributions but does not always increase efficiency due to the costliness and mis-targeting of punishment. However, if the punishment mechanism is modified so that fines are redistributed as rewards to other group members (rather than burned), both contributions and efficiency increase, and the return to contributing becomes positive. For prediction tasks, this suggests that the structure of the punishment mechanism (specifically, whether punishment is redistributive or not) is a key moderator of the efficiency effect. The control (punishment-off) efficiency is not directly reported, but the paper references prior work showing that standard punishment does not increase efficiency over the no-punishment baseline, while redistributive punishment does. The findings are directly relevant for predicting treatment efficiency from game design dimensions, especially the nature of the punishment and reward mechanisms.

column1: The experiment compares the effects of leader-chosen positive (reward) and negative (punishment) incentive schemes in a repeated public goods game. While punishment increases contributions more than rewards, overall team efficiency (measured as the ratio of actual to maximum possible payoff) is slightly higher under rewards than punishment, though the difference is not statistically significant. Leaders earn more under punishment, but teammates earn more under rewards. The most efficient path in terms of aggregate team payoff is when leaders consistently choose rewards. Switching from rewards to punishment increases contributions, but does not improve overall efficiency or team welfare.

Leaders overwhelmingly prefer to use rewards initially, but some switch to punishment if free-riding is high. Punishment schemes (NEG) lead to higher contributions than reward schemes (POS), both for leaders and teammates. However, overall payoffs and efficiency are higher under rewards, because the reward mechanism increases total team surplus (each reward token increases team payoff, while each punishment token reduces it). Leaders benefit more from punishment, but teammates benefit more from rewards. The most efficient outcome (in terms of team payoff relative to the maximum possible) is achieved when leaders stick to rewards throughout. Switching from rewards to punishment increases contributions immediately and persistently, but does not increase efficiency. The effectiveness of incentive schemes is path-dependent and history matters. The study provides direct evidence on how the structure and cost/impact of incentives affect efficiency and payoffs in public goods games with centralized leader-administered incentives.

column1: In strictly one-shot public goods games, the opportunity to sanction or reward other group members does not significantly increase allocative efficiency or average group account contributions compared to the baseline VCM without sanctions or rewards. While subjects do use sanctions and rewards, and these are targeted in expected ways (punishing low contributors, rewarding high contributors), the net effect on efficiency is negligible or slightly negative due to the costs of sanctioning and rewarding. Uncertainty about whether sanctions or rewards will be imposed does not significantly alter these results.

This study finds that in a one-shot voluntary contribution mechanism (VCM) with four players, the introduction of costly opportunities to sanction or reward other group members does not significantly increase group account contributions or allocative efficiency compared to a baseline VCM without such opportunities. The mean allocative efficiency is highest in the baseline (77.37%), and is similar or slightly lower in the sanction and reward treatments, with no statistically significant differences. Subjects do use sanctions and rewards, and these are directed as expected (punishing low contributors, rewarding high contributors), but the costs of these actions offset any potential gains in cooperation, resulting in no net efficiency improvement. Making the imposition of sanctions or rewards uncertain (vs. certain) also has no significant effect on contributions or efficiency.

For prediction tasks, this paper provides strong evidence that in one-shot, four-player, continuous-contribution VCMs with a marginal per-capita return of 0.5, the introduction of costly punishment or reward opportunities does not increase efficiency relative to the control. The costs of punishment and reward offset any behavioral increases in cooperation, resulting in similar or slightly lower efficiency. The results suggest that, in one-shot settings, enabling punishment or reward is unlikely to improve group efficiency, and may even reduce it slightly due to the direct costs incurred. The findings are directly relevant for settings with no repeated interaction, no communication, and anonymous groupings.

column1: The paper finds that the effectiveness of peer reward and punishment in sustaining cooperation and increasing group efficiency in public goods games depends critically on the alignment of local and global incentives. When local group welfare is not improved by cooperation (i.e., locally inefficient), peer reward and punishment fail to sustain high cooperation and group efficiency, even though global welfare would benefit from cooperation. In contrast, when local and global incentives are aligned (locally efficient), peer reward and punishment are effective in sustaining cooperation and increasing group efficiency. The ability to target reward/punishment globally (vs. only locally) also affects outcomes, with more selective rewarding in global conditions but overall lower reward amounts.

The experiment demonstrates that peer reward and punishment can sustain high cooperation and group efficiency in public goods games only when local group welfare is improved by cooperation (locally efficient). In the locally inefficient condition (Local0.1), where cooperation benefits the global group but not the local group, both cooperation and group profit are significantly lower, and peer reward and punishment are less effective. The study provides direct evidence that the alignment of local and global incentives, as well as the scope of peer reward/punishment, are key moderators of the efficiency gains from punishment and reward in public goods games.

This paper provides strong evidence that the effect of enabling punishment (and reward) on group efficiency in public goods games is highly sensitive to the alignment of local and global incentives (i.e., whether cooperation is locally efficient or inefficient). When local group welfare is not improved by cooperation, enabling punishment/reward does not increase efficiency, even if global efficiency would benefit. The scope of punishment/reward (local vs. global) also matters: global targeting allows for more selective rewarding but may reduce the total amount of reward given. For prediction tasks, the paper suggests that the effect of punishment on efficiency will be positive only when local and global incentives are aligned, and that group size and the structure of interaction (localization) are important moderators. Control efficiency (without punishment) is not directly reported, but the relative differences between conditions provide guidance for predicting treatment efficiency.

column1: This paper uses laboratory experiments with an inefficient public goods game (MPCR=0.2, so contributions reduce group welfare) to test the effects of punishment and reward options on contribution and payoffs. Four conditions are tested: no sanctions, punishment only, reward only, and both punishment and reward. The main finding is that the availability of punishment alone does not significantly increase contributions or payoffs, while the availability of reward (with or without punishment) leads to higher contributions and, crucially, higher final payoffs—even though the public good is inefficient. The effect of punishment on efficiency is weak or non-significant, while reward has a strong positive effect. These results hold even when participants are explicitly told and tested on the inefficiency of the public good. The study also finds that participants use rewards to reciprocate high contributions, and that mutual rewarding can sustain inefficient norms and high payoffs.

The experiments show that in an inefficient public goods game (where contributing reduces total group welfare), enabling punishment alone does not significantly increase contributions or group payoffs compared to no-sanction control. In contrast, enabling reward (with or without punishment) leads to higher contributions and, importantly, higher final payoffs, even though the public good is inefficient. This is because mutual rewarding compensates for the losses from inefficient contributions. The effect of punishment on efficiency is weak or non-significant, while reward has a strong positive effect. These findings are robust to explicit instruction and comprehension checks about the inefficiency of the public good. The results suggest that punishment alone is not effective at increasing efficiency in this context, but reward can create positive-sum outcomes through social exchange, even when the underlying norm is inefficient.

column1: The paper finds that both material sanctions (costly punishment/reward) and costless moral judgments increase cooperation and group earnings relative to a control with no sanctions. However, material sanctions reduce efficiency due to their cost, resulting in group earnings that are not significantly higher than control. Moral judgment groups achieve higher efficiency (earnings) than both control and material sanction groups. Thus, punishment increases cooperation but does not improve efficiency, while moral judgments increase both cooperation and efficiency.

In a repeated public goods game with four-person groups, the ability to impose costly material sanctions (punishment/reward) or to make costless moral judgments (approval/disapproval) both increased contributions relative to a control with no sanctions. However, material sanctions led to efficiency losses due to their cost, so group earnings in the material sanction condition were not significantly higher than in the control. In contrast, moral judgment groups earned significantly more than both control and material sanction groups, indicating higher efficiency. The effect of both interventions was present from the first round (deterrence) and persisted across rounds (learning). Material sanctions also led to cycles of retaliation, while moral judgments did not. Downstream, moral judgment groups showed higher trust, trustworthiness, and generosity in subsequent games. Thus, punishment increases cooperation but does not improve efficiency, while moral judgments increase both cooperation and efficiency.

This paper provides strong evidence that enabling costly punishment in a standard PGG increases cooperation but does not improve efficiency, as the cost of punishment offsets the gains from higher contributions. In contrast, costless moral judgments increase both cooperation and efficiency. For prediction, the presence of costly punishment should not be expected to increase average efficiency above control, while costless, non-material sanctions can. The specific game design (4 players, 9 rounds, continuous contributions, MPCR=0.5, punishment cost 1:3, no chat, no knowledge of total rounds) is highly informative for similar lab PGGs. The findings suggest that the efficiency effect of punishment is sensitive to its costliness, and that non-material sanctions may be a more effective and efficient intervention.

column1: The paper finds that introducing opportunities for costly sanctions in a linear public goods game initially reduces efficiency due to the direct costs of sanctioning, but over time, as the threat of sanctioning sustains higher contributions and the use of sanctions declines, group efficiency increases and can surpass the baseline (no-sanction) condition. Reward opportunities alone do not sustain high contributions or efficiency, as the use of rewards decays rapidly. The combination of sanctions and rewards yields the highest contributions and earnings, but the effect is mainly driven by the sanctioning mechanism. The results highlight the importance of punishment for sustaining cooperation and improving efficiency in repeated public goods games, though the cost structure of punishment is critical.

In a repeated linear public goods game with four players and ten rounds per sequence, the introduction of costly sanctioning (punishment) opportunities after an initial baseline phase leads to sustained higher contributions and, after an initial efficiency loss due to sanctioning costs, to higher group efficiency compared to the baseline. Reward opportunities alone do not maintain high contributions or efficiency, as the use of rewards declines quickly. The combination of sanctions and rewards produces the highest average contributions and earnings, but the effect is primarily due to the sanctioning mechanism. The cost structure is linear: each token used for punishment costs the punisher 10 cents and reduces the target's earnings by 10 cents (total group loss: 20 cents per token). The marginal per-capita return (MPCR) is 0.5. Players cannot identify who punished or rewarded them, and all information is anonymous. No communication is allowed. Over time, as the threat of punishment sustains cooperation and the use of punishment declines, efficiency improves. The effect is robust to the absence of communication and anonymity of punishment. The findings suggest that, for similar game designs (4 players, 10 rounds, MPCR=0.5, linear punishment, no chat, anonymous), enabling punishment will increase efficiency relative to the control, especially in later rounds. column1: In repeated public goods games with persistent group identity, enabling costly punishment increases contributions and efficiency relative to a no-punishment control, but reward is equally effective at maintaining cooperation and leads to higher total payoffs. The study finds that in repeated public goods games with fixed groups, both punishment and reward mechanisms can maintain high levels of cooperation and efficiency compared to a control with no targeted interactions. However, reward leads to higher total payoffs than punishment, as punishment is costly and does not increase efficiency beyond what is achieved by reward. When both reward and punishment are available, groups that use reward more achieve higher payoffs, while groups that use punishment more achieve lower payoffs. The results suggest that positive reciprocity (reward) is more effective than negative reciprocity (punishment) for promoting efficiency in repeated public goods games.

The effect of punishment is less positive for efficiency than reward, and when both are available, punishment may even reduce efficiency due to its cost. The findings are most applicable to repeated, fixed-group, non-anonymous settings with continuous contribution choices and no communication.

column1: In this lab experiment, groups of four participants repeatedly choose between a standard public goods game (VCM), a VCM with punishment, and a VCM with reward, and also vote on the effectiveness (leverage) of the sanctioning mechanism. While punishment leads to the highest contributions, it results in lower average profits (efficiency) than both the standard VCM and especially the reward institution. The VCM with reward is both the most preferred and the most efficient institution, even though the maximum leverage for reward is lower than for punishment. Efficiency is highest under reward, intermediate under the standard VCM, and lowest under punishment, due to the costliness of punishment actions.

The experiment shows that, although punishment increases contributions more than reward or the standard VCM, it reduces group efficiency because the costs of punishment outweigh the gains from increased cooperation. The reward institution, despite a lower maximum leverage, is both the most preferred and the most efficient, yielding the highest average profits. The standard VCM yields intermediate efficiency. The effectiveness (leverage) of both punishment and reward increases contributions, but only reward increases efficiency. There is no significant difference in efficiency or institutional choice between partner and stranger matching. Gender differences exist in preferences for institutions, but not in efficiency outcomes.

This paper provides direct evidence that, in a standard linear public goods game with endogenous institution choice, enabling punishment increases contributions but reduces efficiency (average group profit) compared to both the control (standard VCM) and the reward institution. The efficiency loss is due to the cost of punishment actions. The reward institution, even with lower maximum leverage, is more efficient than both punishment and the standard VCM. For prediction, this suggests that, holding control efficiency constant, enabling punishment is likely to decrease efficiency, unless the punishment technology is extremely effective and/or punishment is used sparingly. The effect of punishment on efficiency is robust across partner and stranger matching, and is not moderated by self-selection or communication (which is absent). The paper also shows that increasing the effectiveness of punishment or reward increases contributions, but only reward increases efficiency.

column1: Introducing an endogenously funded, average-oriented punishment and reward mechanism in a two-stage public good game increases both public good provision and average earnings compared to a baseline without the mechanism. The mechanism is voluntarily funded by group members, and its strength is determined by their contributions. Groups over-invest in the mechanism initially, but this over-investment decreases over time. The mechanism leads to higher and more stable group payoffs and public good contributions, with average earnings significantly higher in the mechanism treatment than in the baseline.

The experiment demonstrates that subjects are willing to pay to establish a norm enforcement mechanism that punishes or rewards deviations from the group average contribution. With the mechanism, average group contributions to the public good are substantially higher than in the baseline, and average earnings are also higher. The mechanism is almost always implemented, and its strength (enforcement parameter) is positively associated with higher public good contributions. Over time, groups learn to reduce over-investment in the mechanism. The mechanism treatment results in more stable and higher efficiency (measured as group earnings relative to the maximum possible).

This paper provides direct, high-quality evidence that enabling an endogenous, average-oriented punishment/reward mechanism in a repeated public good game with three players and ten rounds increases both group efficiency and average earnings compared to a control without such a mechanism. The design closely matches standard PGGs, and the efficiency improvement is robust. The findings support predicting a more positive effect of punishment/reward mechanisms on efficiency, especially when the mechanism is endogenously funded and targets deviations from the group average. The results are most directly applicable to small, fixed groups with repeated interaction and endogenous institution formation.

column1: The paper finds that, in a repeated public goods game with and without punishment, teams (especially those using unanimity rule) achieve higher net profits (efficiency) than individuals. This is due to both higher contributions (in the absence of punishment) and lower use of costly punishment (when punishment is available). Anti-social punishment is much less frequent in teams, especially under unanimity. The team decision process dampens extreme preferences for punishment, leading to less resource destruction and higher group welfare.

In a lab experiment comparing individuals and teams (majority and unanimity rule) in a repeated public goods game, teams with unanimity rule contributed more and achieved higher net profits than individuals in the absence of punishment. When punishment was introduced, all groups increased contributions, but teams (especially unanimity teams) used punishment less, particularly anti-social punishment. As a result, teams—especially unanimity teams—achieved higher net profits (efficiency) than individuals. The reduction in punishment was due to both a lower probability of punishing and a lower level of punishment when it occurred. The team decision process, especially under unanimity, filtered out extreme punishment preferences, reducing destructive punishment and increasing efficiency.

This paper provides direct evidence that, in a standard repeated public goods game with punishment, enabling punishment increases efficiency (net profits) for all groups, but the increase is larger for teams using unanimity rule than for individuals. The efficiency gain is due to both higher contributions and less costly punishment, especially less anti-social punishment. The game design dimensions—such as group size (individuals vs. 3-person teams), number of rounds, MPCR, punishment cost and technology, absence of chat, and feedback—are all clearly specified and match standard PGG designs. The findings suggest that, when predicting the effect of punishment on efficiency, team decision rules (especially unanimity) are important moderators: unanimity teams achieve higher efficiency with punishment than individuals, mainly by reducing wasteful punishment. The control (no-punishment) efficiency is also higher for unanimity teams. Thus, for similar designs, enabling punishment is likely to increase efficiency, especially for teams with strong coordination requirements.

column1: This multilab replication of Gürerk et al. (2006) finds that groups with peer sanctioning institutions (SI) consistently achieve higher average profits (efficiency) than groups without sanctioning (SFI) in most labs. The effect is robust across five of seven European labs, with the remaining two showing weaker but still positive results. The design is a public goods game with endogenous institution choice, and the payoff advantage of SI emerges after several rounds as cooperation is sustained by punishment.

Across seven European labs, allowing participants to choose between a sanctioning institution (SI) and a sanctioning-free institution (SFI) in a repeated public goods game leads to the majority of participants migrating to SI. In five labs, SI groups achieve significantly higher average profits and contributions than SFI groups, replicating the original findings. In the other two labs, the effect is weaker but still in the same direction. The payoff advantage of SI emerges after several rounds, as peer punishment sustains cooperation. The results are robust to variations in lab, language, and data collection method, but all parameter settings (e.g., group size, MPCR, punishment cost) are held constant as in the original study.

This paper provides strong evidence that, in a 12-player, 30-round linear public goods game with endogenous institution choice, MPCR of 0.133, and a peer punishment institution with a 1:3 cost-to-impact ratio, enabling punishment leads to higher group efficiency (average profit) compared to no-punishment control. The effect is robust across multiple European labs. The design dimensions are tightly controlled and fixed, so the findings are most directly applicable to similar parameterizations. The paper does not vary key design dimensions (e.g., punishment cost, group size), so it cannot inform how the effect would change under different settings, but it provides a strong baseline for the canonical design.

column1: The paper finds that introducing a strong institution with high punishment and high contribution requirements in a public goods game leads to large increases in group efficiency/payoff, especially for groups composed of non-cooperative types. Under weak or no institution, non-cooperative groups perform poorly, but under a strong institution, their payoffs match those of cooperative groups. However, when institutional strength is determined endogenously by group voting, non-cooperative groups fail to adopt strong institutions and thus do not achieve high efficiency.

In a repeated public goods game, groups of participants pre-sorted by cooperative inclination (high/cooperative vs. low/non-cooperative) played under four conditions: no institution, weak institution (low threshold, low punishment), strong institution (high threshold, high punishment), and evolving institution (parameters set by group voting). Under no or weak institution, non-cooperative groups had much lower payoffs than cooperative groups. Under a strong institution, both group types achieved equally high payoffs, with non-cooperative groups benefiting the most from the institutional change. However, when institutional parameters were set by voting, non-cooperative groups failed to increase punishment and contribution thresholds, resulting in lower payoffs. The results show that strong, externally imposed punishment institutions can solve the 'hard problem' of cooperation and efficiency, but self-governance by non-cooperative groups does not reliably produce such institutions.

This paper provides direct evidence that, in a standard repeated public goods game with four players, 4–16 rounds, and no communication, the introduction of a strong, externally imposed punishment institution (high fine, high contribution threshold, automatic monitoring and punishment) substantially increases group efficiency/payoff, especially for groups with low baseline cooperation. The effect is robust and large: mean payoffs rise from near the Nash equilibrium (10–12 units) to near the social optimum (16.6–16.9 units). However, if the institution's strength is determined by group voting, non-cooperative groups do not adopt strong punishment, and efficiency gains are not realized. For prediction, this paper supports a strong positive effect of punishment on efficiency when punishment is externally imposed and severe, but little or no effect when punishment is weak or endogenous to non-cooperative groups. The design dimensions most critical for this result are punishment cost/tech, the presence of a fixed strong institution, and the absence of communication.

column1: The paper finds that the structure of the punishment network significantly affects public good contributions and sanctioning behavior. However, after accounting for the costs of sanctioning, overall group earnings (efficiency) are similar across punishment and no-punishment networks, with some evidence that punishment does not increase efficiency and may even reduce it in some network structures. The network configuration is more important than the absolute punishment capacity for determining contributions, sanctions, and efficiency.

This study experimentally manipulates punishment network structure and punishment capacity in a repeated linear public goods game with four players per group. Treatments include no-punishment, complete punishment, pairwise punishment, and untouchable punishment networks, as well as variants with increased punishment capacity. The main findings are: (1) Complete punishment networks lead to higher contributions than no-punishment or pairwise networks, but not necessarily higher group earnings after accounting for punishment costs. (2) Pairwise punishment networks are less effective at increasing contributions and do not improve efficiency. (3) Increasing punishment capacity in incomplete networks does not significantly improve contributions or efficiency. (4) The structure of the punishment network is more important than the absolute punishment capacity for group outcomes. (5) Targeted revenge is a major driver of antisocial punishment. (6) The presence of an 'untouchable' (who cannot punish or be punished) does not significantly reduce the willingness of others to contribute, but untouchables contribute less and earn more.

For predicting the effect of enabling punishment on efficiency in public goods games, this paper provides strong evidence that the structure of the punishment network (who can punish whom) is a critical moderator. Enabling punishment in a complete network increases contributions but does not necessarily increase efficiency due to the cost of punishment. Incomplete networks (e.g., pairwise) do not yield efficiency gains and may even reduce efficiency. Increasing punishment capacity without changing network structure does not improve efficiency. Thus, when predicting efficiency with punishment enabled, it is crucial to account for both the network structure and the cost/effectiveness of punishment. Control efficiency (no-punishment) is not a reliable predictor of treatment efficiency unless network structure and punishment costs are considered.

column1: In one-shot public goods games with and without punishment, conducted in urban and rural Russia, the introduction of punishment did not increase cooperation or efficiency. Instead, punishment led to substantial payoff losses in all subject pools, mainly due to high rates of 'misdirected' punishment (punishing cooperators as well as free riders). Thus, punishment undermined group efficiency relative to the no-punishment baseline.

The paper finds that, contrary to much of the previous literature, introducing a punishment option in one-shot public goods games in Russia did not increase cooperation or group efficiency. In fact, average earnings (a direct measure of efficiency) were substantially lower in the punishment condition than in the no-punishment condition across all subject pools. This is attributed to high levels of punishment directed at cooperators as well as free riders, leading to large payoff losses. The effect is robust across urban/rural and young/mature subject pools. The findings are supported by both within-subject and between-subject comparisons, and are further corroborated by similar results in repeated-game settings in Russia.

This paper provides strong evidence that, in one-shot public goods games with a punishment option, the effect of punishment on efficiency can be negative if misdirected punishment is prevalent. The game design here (n=3, one-shot, MPCR=0.5, punishment cost=1, punishment impact=3, no chat, no reward, continuous contributions) is highly informative for predicting efficiency outcomes in similar settings. If the control (no-punishment) efficiency is known, enabling punishment in a similar Russian context is likely to reduce efficiency, not increase it. The findings highlight the importance of considering the prevalence of antisocial punishment and the social context when predicting the effect of punishment on efficiency.

column1: The paper finds that the efficacy of peer punishment in sustaining cooperation and efficiency in public good games is highly sensitive to the feedback format. When feedback is about contributions, efficiency and cooperation are high. When feedback is about earnings, both are significantly lower, despite equivalent information and unchanged punishment opportunities. When both types of feedback are given, efficiency is even lower due to harsher punishment and lack of convergence. Thus, institutional details such as feedback format can strongly moderate the effect of punishment on efficiency.

In a standard public good game with peer punishment, the format of feedback (contribution feedback, earnings feedback, or both) after each round has a large effect on group efficiency and cooperation. Contribution feedback leads to the highest efficiency and contributions, earnings feedback leads to lower efficiency and contributions, and providing both types of feedback leads to the lowest efficiency due to increased punishment and lack of convergence. The punishment mechanism itself (cost and effectiveness) is held constant across treatments. The results show that the same punishment institution can have very different efficiency outcomes depending on how information is presented to participants.

This paper provides strong evidence that the effect of punishment on efficiency in public good games is not only a function of the punishment parameters, but also of the information environment—specifically, the feedback format. For prediction tasks, this means that even with identical game design dimensions and control efficiency, the realized efficiency with punishment can vary dramatically depending on whether feedback is about contributions, earnings, or both. Contribution feedback supports higher efficiency, while earnings feedback undermines it. If both are shown, efficiency can be even lower than with earnings feedback alone. Thus, the 'show_other_summaries' dimension (and its content) is a critical moderator for predicting treatment efficiency.

column1: The paper finds that the effect of peer punishment on efficiency depends critically on the institutional form. In standard (Baseline) and Sequential punishment institutions, the introduction of punishment opportunities increases contributions but reduces net earnings (efficiency) due to high punishment costs. In contrast, a Consensual punishment institution, where punishment is only enacted if at least two group members request it, leads to both higher contributions and higher net earnings, surpassing the no-punishment baseline. Thus, punishment can either harm or enhance efficiency depending on the rules governing its application.

This experiment compares three peer punishment institutions in a repeated public goods game: Baseline (standard, individual punishment), Sequential (punishment with information about others' punishment actions), and Consensual (punishment only enacted if at least two group members request it). All treatments use groups of 5, 20 rounds (10 without punishment, 10 with), no communication, and full information about group contributions and payoffs (but not identities). The marginal per capita return is 0.4. Punishment costs 1 token per point and reduces the target's payoff by 3 tokens per point. The main findings are: (1) Punishment opportunities increase contributions in all treatments, but only the Consensual institution increases net earnings (efficiency) above the no-punishment baseline. In Baseline and Sequential, punishment reduces efficiency due to high punishment costs. (2) The Consensual institution achieves higher cooperation and efficiency with less punishment, as it censors anti-social punishment (punishment of high contributors) and requires consensus to punish. (3) Providing more information about others' punishment actions (Sequential) does not improve coordination or efficiency. (4) The form of the punishment institution is a critical moderator of the efficiency effect of punishment.

This paper provides strong evidence that the efficiency effect of enabling punishment in public goods games is highly sensitive to the institutional details of the punishment mechanism. In standard and sequential punishment settings (where any individual can punish unilaterally), punishment increases contributions but reduces efficiency due to high punishment costs. column1: The introduction of formal sanctioning institutions in a repeated public goods game with endogenous group migration increases average payoffs, efficiency, and reduces payoff inequality, especially when the sanctioning regime is chosen endogenously by group vote. Sanctions lead to higher contributions and payoffs compared to sanction-free groups. Allowing groups to vote on sanctions further increases efficiency and equalizes payoffs across groups, compared to exogenously imposed sanctions.

In a repeated public goods game with two groups and endogenous migration, the presence of formal sanctioning institutions (a fixed fee plus a fine on private account allocations) leads to higher contributions and significantly higher average payoffs compared to sanction-free groups. When only one group has sanctions (No-Voting treatment), that group becomes overpopulated, and payoff inequality emerges. When groups can vote on whether to implement sanctions (Voting treatment), most groups eventually choose sanctions, group sizes become more balanced, migration decreases, and overall efficiency and average payoffs increase further. The ability to endogenously choose institutions (via voting) leads to more efficient and equitable outcomes than exogenously imposed sanctions. The effect of sanctions on efficiency is robust and positive, and the endogenous choice of sanctions amplifies this effect.

This paper provides strong evidence that enabling formal punishment in a repeated PGG with migration increases efficiency and average payoffs, relative to a control without punishment. The effect is even stronger when the sanctioning institution is chosen endogenously by group vote. The design dimensions—such as player count (10, split into two groups of 5), number of rounds (30), absence of chat, continuous contributions, and a formal, automatic punishment mechanism—are all specified. The marginal per-capita return (MPCR) varies with group size but is always less than 1, and the punishment is highly effective (80% fine on private account, plus a fixed fee). There is no reward mechanism. Players are shown summary information about both groups' contributions and rule-sets. The findings suggest that, for similar game designs, enabling punishment will reliably increase efficiency, and allowing endogenous institutional choice (voting) will further boost efficiency and reduce inequality. The control (no-punishment) efficiency is substantially lower than with punishment enabled. This paper is highly informative for predicting treatment efficiency from design dimensions and control efficiency.

column1: The paper finds that introducing peer punishment in repeated linear public goods games increases group efficiency (earnings) in the Take (commission) frame but not in the Give (omission) frame. Punishment is more effective at raising both contributions and efficiency in the Take game, where acts of commission (taking from the group account) are judged more harshly and punished more frequently by group members. In the Give game, punishment increases contributions but does not significantly increase efficiency (earnings), likely due to the costs of punishment offsetting the gains from higher contributions.

In a repeated linear public goods game with four players and 30 rounds (20 with/without punishment), the opportunity for peer punishment increases group contributions in both Give and Take frames. However, only in the Take frame does punishment significantly increase group earnings (efficiency) relative to the no-punishment baseline. In the Give frame, the increase in contributions does not translate into a significant increase in group earnings, as the costs of punishment offset the gains. The effect is driven by more effective targeting of low contributors in the Take game, where acts of commission are punished more harshly and by more group members. The magnitude of punishment per se is not higher in the Take game, but the likelihood of being punished for low contributions is greater. Thus, the efficiency-enhancing effect of punishment is context-dependent, being stronger in environments where non-cooperation is framed as an act of commission.

This paper provides strong evidence that the effect of enabling punishment on efficiency depends on the framing of the social dilemma (Give vs. Take). For games isomorphic to the Take frame (where non-cooperation is an act of commission), enabling punishment is likely to yield a substantial increase in efficiency, as measured by group earnings relative to the social optimum. For standard Give frame public goods games, enabling punishment increases contributions but does not reliably increase efficiency, due to the costliness of punishment. The game design dimensions—player count (4), number of rounds (30), no chat, continuous contributions, MPCR 0.5, punishment cost 1, punishment impact 3, no rewards, full information on round number and others' contributions, but no punishment source identification—are all precisely reported and should be used for prediction. The control efficiency (group earnings in the no-punishment condition) is a strong predictor of the potential for efficiency gains from punishment, especially in Take games where baseline efficiency is lower and punishment is more effective.

column1: The paper analyzes heterogeneity in punishment behavior in repeated public goods games with and without punishment, using data from Herrmann et al. (2008) across 16 global subject pools. It finds that the presence of antisocial punishers (Type AF) in a group is strongly associated with lower group earnings (i.e., lower efficiency), while groups with only free rider punishers (Type F) or non-punishers (Type N) achieve much higher earnings. The share of Type AF subjects varies substantially across cultures and explains much of the cross-cultural variation in the effectiveness of peer punishment. Thus, the effect of punishment on efficiency is highly context-dependent: in groups/cultures with many antisocial punishers, punishment reduces efficiency, while in groups with only free rider punishers, punishment is more effective at sustaining cooperation and efficiency.

This paper shows that the effectiveness of peer punishment in public goods games is highly heterogeneous and depends critically on the composition of punishment types within groups. Using a finite mixture model, the authors classify subjects into three types: non-punishers (Type N), antisocial/free rider punishers (Type AF), and free rider-only punishers (Type F). The presence of Type AF subjects, who punish both low and high contributors, is strongly associated with lower group earnings and reduced efficiency. In contrast, groups with only Type F and Type N subjects achieve much higher efficiency. The number of Type AF subjects in a group explains a large share of the variance in group earnings, more than baseline cooperativeness or period effects. Cross-cultural differences in the prevalence of Type AF subjects explain much of the observed variation in the effectiveness of punishment across societies.

For predicting the effect of enabling punishment on efficiency in public goods games, this paper provides strong evidence that the effect is not uniform: it depends on the prevalence of antisocial punishers (Type AF) in the group or population. In environments where antisocial punishment is common, enabling punishment can substantially reduce efficiency. In environments where only free rider punishment occurs, enabling punishment can increase or sustain efficiency. The paper provides quantitative evidence (e.g., groups with four Type AF subjects earn 68.7% less than groups with only Type F/N) and regression models showing that the number of Type AF subjects is a strong predictor of group earnings. Thus, for prediction, the cultural or group composition regarding punishment types is a critical moderator, and control game efficiency alone is insufficient to predict treatment efficiency without considering this heterogeneity.

column1: This paper reports a lab-in-the-field experiment in rural China with a repeated public goods game with punishment, manipulating group ethnic composition. The main finding is that in ethnically mixed groups, participants are less willing to punish in-group (co-ethnic) free-riders, which undermines the credibility of punishment and leads to lower contributions and lower group earnings (efficiency) compared to homogeneous groups. Thus, the presence of ethnic diversity and in-group favoritism in punishment harms both cooperation and efficiency.

The experiment finds that in public goods games with punishment, ethnically mixed groups experience lower contributions and lower group earnings than homogeneous groups. This is primarily because participants are less likely to punish co-ethnic free-riders when out-group members are present, reducing the deterrent effect of punishment. The effect is strongest in unbalanced mixed groups (3+1 composition), where efficiency losses are largest. The study provides direct evidence that the effectiveness of punishment as a cooperation-enforcing institution is undermined by in-group favoritism in diverse groups, leading to lower efficiency.

This paper provides strong evidence that, in public goods games with punishment, the efficiency gains from punishment are reduced or even reversed in ethnically mixed groups due to in-group favoritism in punishment assignment. When predicting the effect of enabling punishment on efficiency, the group composition (homogeneous vs mixed) is a critical moderator: punishment is less effective (or even harmful) in mixed groups because in-group members are less likely to punish each other, reducing deterrence and lowering contributions and earnings. The game uses standard PGG parameters (4 players, 5 rounds, MPCR=0.5, punishment cost=2, punishment impact=5, no chat, no rewards, anonymous punishment). Control efficiency (without punishment) is not directly reported, but the main comparison is between group types with punishment enabled. The findings suggest that, holding other design dimensions constant, enabling punishment in mixed-ethnicity groups may not increase efficiency and can even decrease it relative to homogeneous groups.

column1: The paper finds that providing social history (information about the outcomes of a previous experiment) increases both the acceptance and the efficiency of a peer punishment institution in a public goods game. With social history, subjects are more likely to join the punishment institution, cooperate at higher levels, and achieve higher payoffs and efficiency more quickly and stably than without social history. The efficiency of the punishment institution is higher both in the short and long run when social learning is enabled by social history.

The experiment demonstrates that endogenously chosen punishment institutions in a repeated public goods game become more efficient and more widely accepted when participants are provided with social history (detailed information about the outcomes of a previous cohort). Social history leads to higher initial acceptance of the punishment institution, higher initial and sustained contributions, lower punishment expenses, and higher average payoffs. The efficiency (measured as surplus ratio and average payoff) is significantly higher in the social history treatment than in the baseline. Cash penalties are more effective than token penalties at increasing both contributions and earnings, especially in the early rounds, but the difference between cash and token punishment diminishes over time. The deterrent effect of punishment is strong enough to compensate for the deadweight loss from penalties, resulting in higher overall group welfare. The results suggest that the tangibility of punishment (cash vs. digital) matters for short-run deterrence, but adaptation reduces this effect with experience.

column1: The paper finds that punishment generally increases collective payoff and cooperation, but the effect depends on the size of the punishment and the cognitive ability of group members. In repeated PGGs, small punishment can actually reduce efficiency for high cognitive ability groups, while large punishment increases efficiency for both high and low cognitive ability groups. In one-shot PGGs, punishment increases cooperation and collective payoff for both groups, with no significant difference between cognitive ability groups except under large punishment.

This paper experimentally studies the effects of punishment (none, small, large) on efficiency (collective payoff) in both one-shot and repeated public goods games with groups of four. It finds that: (1) In one-shot PGGs, both small and large punishment increase collective payoff compared to no punishment, with large punishment having a stronger effect. Cognitive ability does not significantly affect efficiency except under large punishment, where high cognitive ability groups achieve higher payoffs. (2) In repeated PGGs, the effect of punishment is more complex: small punishment can reduce efficiency for high cognitive ability groups (who contribute less than in the no-punishment baseline), while large punishment increases efficiency for both high and low cognitive ability groups. Thus, the effect of punishment on efficiency is not always positive and depends on both the magnitude of punishment and group cognitive composition.

For prediction tasks, this paper provides direct evidence that the effect of punishment on efficiency in PGGs depends on the punishment magnitude and the cognitive ability of participants. Small punishment may not always increase efficiency and can even reduce it in repeated games with high cognitive ability groups. Large punishment reliably increases efficiency. The game design dimensions most relevant here are player_count (4), num_rounds (1 for one-shot, 10 for repeated), mpcr (0.5), punishment_cost (institutional, fixed, not paid by peers), and punishment_tech (penalty for under-contribution, with two levels: small and large). There is no chat, no reward, and players receive feedback about others' investments. The findings suggest that, for similar lab PGGs with institutional punishment, enabling large punishment will increase efficiency, but enabling only small punishment may not, especially in repeated settings with high cognitive ability participants.

column1: This paper experimentally demonstrates that combining costly punishment with indirect reciprocity (reputation) in a public goods game increases efficiency compared to punishment alone. The interaction reduces the frequency and cost of punishment, concentrates it on free-riders, and boosts both cooperation and group payoffs. Efficiency is higher in the combined treatment (PUN&IR) than in the punishment-only treatment (PUN), and both are higher than in the absence of punishment.

The study finds that when participants can choose between groups with or without costly punishment, and with or without an indirect reciprocity (reputation) mechanism, most eventually prefer the group with both punishment and reputation. The combination (PUN&IR) leads to higher contributions, more efficient use of punishment (less frequent, more targeted), and significantly higher efficiency (group payoff as a fraction of the social optimum) than punishment alone (PUN). The destructive effect of punishment on efficiency is largely mitigated by the presence of reputation, as punishment is used less but more effectively. Full contributors in the combined treatment achieve payoffs close to the social optimum, and even the least cooperative subjects are more cooperative in the combined treatment. The results suggest that punishment and reputation are complementary, not substitutes, and their interaction provides a low-cost, high-efficiency solution to social dilemmas.

column1: The paper finds that the availability of both monetary (formal) and nonmonetary (informal) sanctions in a public goods game (VCM) leads to higher group earnings (efficiency/welfare) than either type of sanction alone. In a repeated public goods game with groups of 4 over 15 rounds, three treatments were compared: monetary punishment (MP), nonmonetary punishment (NP), and both punishments (BP). All sanctioning systems increased contributions and welfare relative to no-sanction baselines from prior literature. NP (informal) sanctions alone initially produced high welfare but lost effectiveness over time. MP (monetary) sanctions sustained higher contributions but incurred enforcement costs, reducing efficiency. The BP treatment, combining both, resulted in the highest group earnings and contributions in the later rounds, with lower deadweight loss from punishment than MP. The combined system allows for nuanced sanctioning, using costless informal sanctions when effective and costly formal sanctions when needed, maximizing efficiency.

column1: Introducing mild legal (centralized) sanctions in addition to social (decentralized) punishment in a one-shot public goods game increases total group efficiency (mean payoff) by 33%. Legal sanctions partially crowd out social punishment, but the combined effect is higher cooperation and lower social sanctioning costs, resulting in a substantial net welfare gain.

In LAW, legal sanctions are nondeterrent in isolation but, when combined with social punishment, they increase cooperation (mean contribution rises from 11.8 to 15.1 out of 20) and total efficiency (mean payoff rises from 18.59 to 24.65, a 33% increase). Social punishment is partially crowded out (mean punishment points drop by 57%), but the overall cost of norm enforcement falls and group welfare rises. The design dimensions (player count, MPCR, punishment cost/tech, no chat, continuous contributions, etc.) are all clearly specified, making this study highly informative for predicting efficiency outcomes in similar game designs.

column1: The paper provides strong experimental evidence that the availability of a sanctioning (punishment) institution in a public goods game leads to much higher efficiency and group payoffs compared to a sanction-free institution. Over time, nearly all participants migrate to the sanctioning institution, where cooperation and efficiency approach the theoretical maximum, while the sanction-free institution collapses to zero cooperation and efficiency.

In a repeated public goods game with endogenous institution choice, participants could choose between a sanctioning institution (with both positive and negative sanctions) and a sanction-free institution. Initially, most participants preferred the sanction-free institution, but over time, nearly all migrated to the sanctioning institution. In the sanctioning institution, cooperation and efficiency increased steadily, reaching over 95% of the maximum possible group payoff in the final period, while the sanction-free institution's efficiency fell to zero. The presence of punishment (negative sanctions) was the key driver of sustained high cooperation and efficiency. The study demonstrates that sanctioning institutions have a strong competitive advantage and can resolve the social dilemma by attracting and converting even initially noncooperative individuals.

This paper provides direct, high-quality evidence that enabling punishment in a public goods game dramatically increases efficiency compared to a control condition without punishment, even when participants can freely choose between institutions. The design closely matches canonical PGGs, and the efficiency outcome is explicitly measured. The findings support strong positive predictions for the effect of punishment on efficiency, especially in repeated games with migration or institution choice. The specific punishment cost and effectiveness parameters, as well as the presence of both positive and negative sanctions, are informative for parameterizing prediction models.

column1: The paper finds that in a standard linear public goods game with all-or-nothing contributions, the effect of enabling costly punishment on efficiency (average net payoffs) depends critically on the monitoring environment and the severity of punishment. Under perfect monitoring, punishment (especially strong punishment) increases both cooperation and efficiency. Under imperfect (noisy) monitoring, standard punishment reduces efficiency below the no-punishment baseline, while strong punishment restores efficiency to the no-punishment level but does not improve it. Thus, the effect of punishment on efficiency is positive under perfect monitoring, negative or neutral under imperfect monitoring, and non-monotonic in punishment severity when monitoring is imperfect.

In 50-round, three-player public goods games with all-or-nothing contributions, the introduction of costly punishment options has different effects depending on monitoring and punishment severity. With perfect monitoring, both regular and strong punishment increase average net payoffs, with stronger punishment yielding higher efficiency. With imperfect (noisy) monitoring, regular punishment reduces efficiency below the no-punishment baseline, while strong punishment increases cooperation but only restores efficiency to the no-punishment level (i.e., the gains from increased cooperation are offset by the costs of punishment). The relationship between punishment severity and efficiency is U-shaped under noise: intermediate punishment is worst for efficiency, while strong punishment is neutral. The paper provides direct, quantitative evidence on efficiency outcomes for each treatment.

This paper provides high-quality, directly relevant evidence for predicting the effect of punishment on efficiency in public goods games, especially as a function of monitoring quality and punishment severity. It shows that the effect of punishment on efficiency is not always positive: under imperfect monitoring, standard punishment can reduce efficiency, and only very strong punishment can (at best) restore efficiency to the no-punishment baseline. The results are directly applicable to settings with all-or-nothing contributions, 3 players, 50 rounds, and known MPCR and punishment parameters. The findings highlight the importance of monitoring quality and punishment effectiveness in predicting efficiency outcomes.

column1: The paper provides strong experimental evidence that introducing costly punishment opportunities in a standard public goods game leads to large and sustained increases in cooperation and, after an initial adjustment period, to higher group efficiency (average group payoff) compared to the no-punishment baseline. In the final periods, the relative payoff gain from punishment is about 20% in the Partner-treatment and 10% in the Stranger-treatment. Punishment is targeted at free-riders and is effective at raising their contributions, which in turn increases group welfare.

Introducing a costly punishment option in a repeated public goods game with groups of four, a known 10-round horizon, and no communication or identification, leads to a dramatic increase in average contributions and, after an initial period of adjustment, to higher group efficiency (payoff) compared to the no-punishment baseline. In the no-punishment condition, contributions and efficiency decline toward full free-riding. In the punishment condition, contributions are sustained at high levels (often near full cooperation), and group payoffs in the final periods are 10-20% higher than in the control. Punishment is used primarily against those who contribute less than the group average, and punished individuals tend to increase their contributions in subsequent rounds. The effect is robust across both stranger (random rematching) and partner (fixed group) treatments.

This paper provides direct, high-quality evidence for predicting the effect of enabling costly punishment in a standard linear public goods game with four players, ten rounds, no communication, and anonymous interactions. If the control (no-punishment) efficiency is low (due to declining contributions), enabling punishment is likely to increase efficiency by 10-20% in the final rounds, with the effect being stronger in fixed groups (partner) than in random groups (stranger). The design dimensions (player count, rounds, no chat, continuous contributions, known horizon, full feedback, anonymous punishment) closely match the canonical prediction task, making this paper highly informative for forecasting efficiency outcomes when punishment is enabled.

column1: Introducing noise into the punishment technology in a repeated public goods game leads to a substantial decrease in group efficiency and welfare. As punishment becomes more stochastic (noisy), average payoffs drop, contributions decrease, and punishment efforts (including antisocial punishment) increase. The negative effect on efficiency is monotonic with noise amplitude.

The paper finds that stochastic (noisy) punishment in a repeated public goods game significantly reduces group efficiency and welfare compared to deterministic punishment. As the noise in the punishment multiplier increases (while keeping the mean constant), average payoffs per round drop sharply (from 10.1 MU in control to 5.6 MU in high noise), contributions decrease, and both the frequency and intensity of punishment rise. Notably, antisocial punishment (punishing cooperators) becomes more prevalent under noise, further undermining cooperation and group payoffs. Regression analyses confirm that the negative effect of noise on payoffs is mediated by increased antisocial punishment and reduced contributions.

This paper provides strong evidence that, in a standard repeated PGG with punishment, introducing noise into the punishment technology (i.e., making the punishment impact stochastic rather than deterministic) leads to a substantial and monotonic reduction in efficiency, even when the mean punishment impact is held constant. For prediction tasks, this suggests that the presence and degree of punishment noise is a critical moderator: efficiency gains from enabling punishment are much lower (or even negative) when punishment is noisy. The findings are directly relevant for settings with deterministic punishment (high efficiency) versus noisy punishment (low efficiency), holding other design dimensions constant. The results also highlight the importance of antisocial punishment as a mechanism for efficiency loss under noisy punishment.

column1: The introduction of individual punishment (and reward) mechanisms in a standard public goods game increases both contributions and net payoffs compared to the baseline without such mechanisms. Punishment is particularly effective at sustaining or increasing contributions over time, and net payoffs are higher in treatments with rewards (due to the payoff-increasing nature of the reward mechanism), but also higher in punishment treatments than in the baseline. The presence of a leader (leading by example) does not further increase efficiency or contributions beyond what is achieved by the introduction of punishment or reward mechanisms.

In a repeated public goods game with four players and 20 rounds, the addition of individual punishment or reward mechanisms (either centralized via a leader or decentralized among peers) leads to significantly higher contributions and higher net payoffs compared to the baseline game without such mechanisms. The marginal per capita return is 0.4. Punishment is more effective than reward at sustaining high contributions over time, especially in the peer punishment treatment, where contributions even increase in the second half of the game. Net payoffs are highest in reward treatments (due to the reward mechanism's structure), but also higher in punishment treatments than in the baseline. The presence of a leader (who contributes first and can reward or punish) does not further increase contributions or payoffs compared to peer-based reward or punishment. The effect of punishment on increasing contributions and payoffs is robust, and punishment from leaders has a stronger effect on subsequent contributions than peer punishment. Anti-social punishment is less frequent when punishment is centralized with a leader.

This paper provides strong evidence that, in a standard linear public goods game with four players and 20 rounds, enabling individual punishment (with a cost/impact ratio of 1:3) increases both contributions and net payoffs (i.e., efficiency) compared to the baseline without punishment. The effect is robust whether punishment is centralized (leader) or decentralized (peers), and is not further enhanced by adding a leader who leads by example. The control (no punishment) efficiency is lower than in the punishment-enabled treatments. The findings support the prediction that, holding game design dimensions constant, enabling punishment will increase average efficiency. The specific cost and impact structure (1 point cost reduces target by 3 points) is important for generalization. Reward mechanisms also increase efficiency, but the structure of the reward mechanism in this experiment is payoff-increasing by design. The results are directly relevant for predicting the effect of punishment on efficiency in similar public goods game environments.

column1: This paper studies a public goods game where groups can endogenously choose (via costly voting) whether to supplement the standard VCM with punishment or reward options, and compares this to exogenously imposed institutions. Both punishment and reward can be implemented with low or high effectiveness (leverage). The main findings are: (1) Endogenous institutional choice (voting) increases cooperation and group profits compared to exogenous imposition of the same institution. (2) Punishment and reward both increase contributions and profits relative to the standard VCM, especially when highly effective. (3) Groups overwhelmingly prefer reward over punishment when both are highly effective, and prefer the standard VCM when effectiveness is low. (4) Punishment is rarely chosen endogenously, even though it is effective at raising contributions. (5) Efficiency gains from punishment are limited by its cost, while reward with high leverage yields the highest group profits.

Both punishment and reward options increase contributions and profits compared to the standard VCM, but the effect is much stronger when the punishment/reward technology is highly effective (high leverage). column1: The paper finds that while punishment can maintain high contributions in public good games, the combination of unequal and unstable punishment power (where the strong punisher role can change between rounds) leads to increased competition, excessive punishment, and lower group efficiency (payoff) compared to equal, stable punishment power. When the strong role is assigned based on prosocial behavior, the negative effect on efficiency is less pronounced, but resource waste through punishment persists.

Across three lab experiments, the authors show that in standard public good games with punishment, group efficiency is higher when punishment power is equal and stable. When punishment power is both unequal (one strong punisher, three weak) and unstable (the strong role can change based on performance or prosociality), groups experience more punishment, similar or lower contributions, and significantly lower efficiency (average round win). The negative effect on efficiency is robust to whether the strong role is assigned based on selfish or prosocial behavior. The detrimental effect is not due to inequality alone, but to the combination of inequality and instability, which triggers a 'race for power' and resource waste.

This paper provides strong evidence that, in public good games with punishment, introducing instability in the assignment of punishment power (especially when combined with inequality in punishment effectiveness) reduces group efficiency compared to stable, equal punishment power. For prediction, if the control (punishment disabled) efficiency is known, enabling punishment with equal, stable power is likely to increase efficiency, but enabling punishment with unequal, unstable power is likely to decrease efficiency relative to the equal, stable punishment case. The effect is driven by increased competitive punishment rather than increased cooperation. The findings are directly relevant for settings with 4 players, 10 rounds, continuous contributions, no chat, and full feedback on others' actions.
