column1: The paper finds that the effect of punishment on efficiency in public goods games depends strongly on the network architecture that determines who can monitor and punish whom. While punishment generally increases contributions, its effect on efficiency is more nuanced: some network structures (e.g., complete and certain connected networks) achieve higher efficiency due to lower punishment expenditures, while others (e.g., directed or disconnected networks) suffer from excessive punishment and lower efficiency. The relationship between network structure, punishment, and efficiency is non-monotonic and context-dependent.

This paper experimentally studies public goods games with costly punishment under eight different network architectures, varying completeness, connectedness, and directedness. All games have four players, 15 rounds, and fixed MPCR and punishment cost. The main finding is that network structure crucially moderates the effect of punishment on both cooperation and efficiency. Complete and some connected networks achieve high efficiency because they elicit high contributions with relatively low punishment expenditures. In contrast, directed and disconnected networks often see more punishment and lower efficiency, despite sometimes higher contributions. The marginal benefit of adding monitoring edges is non-linear: adding edges to sparse networks increases efficiency, but in denser networks, more edges can actually reduce efficiency due to over-punishment. The paper provides direct evidence that the efficiency impact of punishment is not uniform but depends on the monitoring/punishment network.

For predicting the efficiency impact of punishment in public goods games, this paper provides strong evidence that network architecture (who can punish whom) is a critical moderator. In games with complete or well-connected networks, punishment increases contributions and can improve efficiency, especially when punishment expenditures are low. In directed or disconnected networks, punishment is more frequent and severe, often reducing efficiency due to high punishment costs. The marginal per-capita return (MPCR), punishment cost, and other game parameters are held constant, so the findings isolate the effect of network structure. When using control efficiency to predict treatment efficiency, one must account for the network's connectedness, completeness, and directedness, as these determine whether punishment will be efficiency-enhancing or not. The results suggest that simply enabling punishment does not guarantee higher efficiency

Exceptions are rare and occur mainly when punishment is used very sparingly and cooperation is already high. For prediction tasks, the presence of costly punishment should generally be expected to lower efficiency relative to control, unless the design or context strongly favors efficient, low-use punishment. The paper also highlights that the marginal per-capita return (MPCR) and matching protocol (reputation effects) can moderate the effect, but the main driver is the costliness and frequency of punishment.

column1: Introducing judicial error (either type I or type II) into a public goods game with formal, centralized punishment reduces both cooperation and group efficiency. The efficiency loss is greater when errors are more frequent and when errors turn a deterrent sanction regime into a non-deterrent one.

When judicial errors are introduced (either type I or type II), both cooperation and efficiency decline. The effect on efficiency is more negative for type I errors than for type II errors, due to the wasteful punishment of cooperators. The negative effect of errors is stronger when the error probability is higher and when errors convert a deterrent sanction regime into a non-deterrent one. The effects of type I and type II errors on contributions are symmetric, but type I errors reduce group earnings more. Subjects show a clear preference for avoiding type I errors, but this preference is fully explained by income maximization rather than additional psychological aversion.

column1: The paper finds that the effect of introducing punishment on efficiency in public goods games depends on group ethnic composition and cultural background. Punishment increases efficiency (measured as the marginal effect of punishment on contribution) in all-Han and mixed-ethnicity groups, but is inefficient in all-Mongolian groups. Ethnic diversity (mixed groups) boosts the efficiency of punishment for both Han and Mongolian Chinese, while punishment is least efficient in all-Mongolian groups due to harsher within-group punishment rooted in cultural norms.

This laboratory experiment with Han Chinese and Mongolian Chinese students uses a standard public goods game with and without a costly punishment stage. Each group has 4 players, and each subject plays 10 rounds without punishment and 10 rounds with punishment. The marginal per-capita return (MPCR) is 0.4. Punishment costs 1 token to the punisher and reduces the punished's payoff by 3 tokens. The main findings are: (1) Punishment increases mean contribution in all treatments, but the efficiency of punishment (measured as the increase in contribution per unit of punishment) varies by group composition. (2) In all-Han and mixed-ethnicity groups, punishment is efficient (marginal effect > 1), while in all-Mongolian groups, punishment is inefficient (marginal effect < 1). (3) Ethnic diversity (mixed groups) boosts punishment efficiency for both Han and Mongolian Chinese. (4) Mongolian Chinese punish more harshly within their own group due to cultural norms ('Anda' tradition), leading to lower efficiency. (5) Han Chinese show strong ingroup bias, contributing more in all-Han groups, especially with punishment. (6) Cultural fusion (Mongolian Chinese with Han cultural background) increases contribution in mixed groups. (7) Overall, the effect of punishment on efficiency is positive in all-Han and mixed groups, but not in all-Mongolian groups.

For games with 4 players, 10 rounds, MPCR 0.4, and a punishment cost/impact ratio of 1:3, punishment increases efficiency in all-Han and mixed-ethnicity groups (marginal effect > 1), but is inefficient in all-Mongolian groups (marginal effect < 1). If the control (no-punishment) efficiency is known, the expected efficiency with punishment will increase substantially in all-Han and mixed groups, but only modestly or not at all in all-Mongolian groups. The results are robust to a 'clear-cut' Han Chinese sample. column1: The paper finds that introducing third-party punishment (via a B-type player) in a public good game increases cooperation, but the way the institution is implemented (endogenously by majority vote vs. exogenously imposed) affects punishment severity and its effectiveness. Endogenous (voted-in) punishment is milder but more effective per unit, while exogenous punishment is harsher. Despite these differences, overall group efficiency (total payoffs) does not differ significantly between endogenous and exogenous punishment institutions. Thus, the efficiency effect of enabling punishment is positive relative to no-punishment, but the method of institution selection (endogenous vs. exogenous) does not significantly alter efficiency.

In a repeated public good game with binary (all-or-nothing) contributions, groups could vote to introduce a third-party punishment institution. When punishment was enabled, a B-type player could assign costly deduction points to defectors (non-contributors), with each deduction point costing the punisher 1 point and reducing the defector's income by 3 points. The main experimental manipulation was whether the punishment institution was implemented endogenously (by majority vote) or exogenously (by random assignment, sometimes overruling the vote). The study finds that: (1) Punishment is significantly milder when the institution is endogenously chosen, but is more effective in inducing cooperation per unit of punishment

column1: The paper finds that in heterogeneous public goods games, the combination of communication and punishment leads to higher group earnings (efficiency) than either instrument alone. However, even with both instruments, groups rarely achieve full efficiency, as most covenants (agreements) strike a compromise between efficiency and equality. Early communication is critical: when communication precedes punishment, groups are more likely to establish covenants, avoid costly feuds, and achieve higher earnings. Late communication, after a history of punishment, is less effective at improving efficiency. The main limitation to efficiency is the persistent concern for equality among group members, even when inequality is justified by prior real-effort performance.

In a lab experiment with heterogeneous groups (different returns from the public good), the authors compare three treatments: (1) communication and punishment available together (ComEarly), (2) punishment first, then communication added later (ComLate), and (3) communication only (ComOnly). Efficiency, measured as group earnings relative to the maximum possible, is highest when both communication and punishment are available from the start (ComEarly: 87% of maximum), lower with only one instrument (ComLate: 60-68%
column2: ComOnly: 76% in part 1, 60% overall). However, even with both instruments, most groups do not achieve full efficiency, as covenants typically require compromise between efficiency and equality. Early communication is crucial: it enables groups to establish covenants and avoid costly punishment cycles (feuds), leading to higher efficiency. Late communication cannot fully overcome the negative effects of prior sanctioning. The study demonstrates that while punishment and communication together improve efficiency, concerns for equality limit the ability of heterogeneous groups to reach the social optimum.

The timing of communication is a key moderator: early communication (before punishment) is much more effective at raising efficiency than late communication. column1: The paper finds that peer punishment in a linear public goods game with heterogeneous endowments increases cooperation and group earnings when endowments are observable (complete information), but is less effective when endowments are private (incomplete information). Under incomplete information, groups enforce a lower contribution norm (contribute-the-Low-endowment), which allows high-endowment members to hide and contribute less, resulting in lower group efficiency compared to the complete information condition. Thus, punishment improves efficiency relative to no punishment, but its effectiveness is attenuated by incomplete information.

In a repeated linear public goods game with two high-endowment and two low-endowment players per group, and costly peer punishment, the ability to observe others' endowments (complete information) leads to the emergence and enforcement of efficient 'contribute-your-endowment' norms. This results in higher contributions and group earnings, especially from high-endowment players, and higher payoffs for low-endowment players. When endowments are private (incomplete information), groups adapt by enforcing a 'contribute-the-Low-endowment' norm, primarily enforced by low-endowment players. This norm prevents total unraveling of cooperation but enables high-endowment players to mimic low-endowment behavior and contribute less, reducing group efficiency. The expected costs and payoffs of noncompliance are explicitly estimated, showing that punishment is less targeted and less effective at sustaining high efficiency under incomplete information.

This paper provides direct evidence that the effectiveness of punishment in increasing efficiency in public goods games depends critically on the information structure. When group members can observe both contributions and endowments, punishment supports high efficiency by enabling enforcement of optimal contribution norms. When endowments are unobservable, punishment still deters total free-riding but cannot sustain full efficiency, as high-endowment members can hide behind the low-endowment norm. For prediction, this means that the presence of punishment will increase efficiency relative to no punishment, but the magnitude of the effect is moderated by whether individual capacities (endowments) are observable. The paper also provides detailed parameterization of the punishment technology and payoff structure, which can be used to calibrate predictive models.

column1: Exogenous probabilistic punishment in a public goods game increases both cooperation and group efficiency (average payoff) compared to no-punishment baseline. However, the efficiency gains depend on the probability and severity of punishment: a 50% probability of a moderate punishment (20 points) yields the highest efficiency, while a low probability of a severe punishment (20% chance of 50 points) does not improve efficiency over baseline. All punishment treatments have the same expected penalty, but their effects on efficiency differ, showing that the structure of punishment (not just expected value) matters.

The study finds that introducing an exogenous, probabilistic punishment mechanism in a repeated public goods game significantly increases both contributions and average payoffs (efficiency) compared to a control with no punishment. Among three punishment treatments with equal expected penalty (10 points), the treatment with a 50% probability of a 20-point punishment produces the highest average payoff and contribution, outperforming both a 100% probability of a 10-point punishment and a 20% probability of a 50-point punishment. The 20% probability/50-point punishment treatment does not significantly increase efficiency over the control. The results show an inverse-U relationship between punishment probability and efficiency, given constant expected penalty. The findings highlight that the design of the punishment mechanism (probability and severity) crucially affects efficiency, not just the expected value of punishment.

This paper provides strong evidence that, in a standard linear public goods game with exogenous, automatic punishment for the lowest contributor, enabling punishment increases efficiency compared to no-punishment baseline, but the magnitude of the effect depends on the probability and severity of punishment. For prediction, the presence of exogenous punishment (with moderate probability and severity) should be expected to increase efficiency, but low-probability, high-severity punishment may not improve efficiency over baseline. The results also show that the structure of punishment (probability vs. severity) matters even when expected penalty is held constant. The findings are directly relevant for predicting treatment efficiency from game design dimensions and control efficiency in similar lab PGGs.

column1: Allowing groups to vote on formal sanction schemes in a linear public goods game leads most groups to quickly select efficient penalty parameters, resulting in significantly higher contributions and group earnings (efficiency) compared to a baseline with no sanctions. The effect is robust across most groups, with only one group failing to converge to efficient rules. The study provides direct evidence that endogenous formal sanctions, when well-designed, can resolve the free-rider problem and sustain high efficiency.

The paper finds that when groups in a linear public goods game are allowed to vote on the parameters of a formal sanction scheme (who is penalized, maximum penalty, and exemption level), most groups quickly learn to select efficient penalty rules that induce full cooperation and maximize group earnings. In the baseline (no sanctions), contributions and earnings decline over time as expected. In the penalty treatment, after voting, contributions and earnings rise and are sustained at high levels, with the median group achieving full cooperation and maximum efficiency. The effect is attributed to the ability of groups to endogenously select strong, well-targeted penalties for free-riding. Individual differences (cooperative orientation, IQ, political conservatism, gender) predict voting behavior, but do not prevent most groups from converging to efficient outcomes.

This paper provides strong, direct evidence that enabling groups to endogenously design formal sanction schemes in a standard linear public goods game can transform a low-efficiency baseline into a high-efficiency outcome. The effect is robust to group heterogeneity and persists over repeated rounds. For prediction, the presence of a formal, group-voted punishment mechanism with high penalty rates and full exemption for full contributors is highly likely to increase efficiency relative to a no-punishment baseline, provided the group can select the parameters. The findings are most applicable to settings with 5 players, 24 rounds, no chat, continuous contributions, and full information about group outcomes.

column1: The paper finds that allowing punishment in a standard public goods game with homogeneous returns (no normative conflict) increases both cooperation and group efficiency (earnings) compared to a no-punishment baseline. However, when normative conflict is introduced (via heterogeneous returns from the public good), punishment increases cooperation but does not increase efficiency, because the costs of feuding (mutual, retaliatory punishment) fully offset the gains from higher contributions. Thus, the effect of punishment on efficiency is positive in homogeneous groups but null in heterogeneous groups with normative conflict.

In a lab public goods game, groups of four played 10 rounds with or without punishment. In the 'Symmetric' treatment (all players have the same marginal per-capita return), punishment opportunities led to higher contributions and significantly higher group earnings (efficiency) compared to the no-punishment baseline. In the 'Asymmetric' treatment (two players have high, two have low returns), punishment also increased contributions, but the frequency and severity of counter-punishment and feuds rose sharply, leading to high punishment costs. As a result, group earnings in the Asymmetric treatment with punishment were not significantly higher than in the no-punishment baseline. The study demonstrates that the efficiency benefits of punishment depend critically on the absence of normative conflict: when such conflict is present, punishment can fail to improve, or even reduce, efficiency due to costly feuding.

This paper provides direct evidence that the efficiency effect of enabling punishment in public goods games depends on group homogeneity and the presence of normative conflict. In symmetric (homogeneous) groups, enabling punishment increases efficiency relative to the no-punishment baseline. In asymmetric (heterogeneous) groups with normative conflict, enabling punishment increases cooperation but not efficiency, as punishment costs (especially from feuds) offset the gains. For prediction, the presence of heterogeneity in returns (or other sources of normative conflict) is a key moderator: control efficiency alone is not sufficient—one must also consider whether the game design induces normative conflict. Other design dimensions (e.g., punishment cost, technology, player count) are held constant in this study, so the main actionable moderator is the symmetry/asymmetry of returns.

column1: The paper finds that introducing a delegated punishment mechanism ('gun for hire') in a linear public goods game increases group welfare (net earnings) by 15–40% compared to peer-to-peer punishment. Delegated punishment is preferred by subjects, is implemented over 70% of the time when available, and crowds out costly peer-to-peer punishment. The efficiency gains are due to both higher contributions and, more importantly, lower punishment costs.

In repeated linear public goods games with four players, the introduction of a delegated punishment mechanism (either imposed or endogenously hired) leads to a substantial and immediate increase in both contributions and net earnings (welfare), compared to both the no-punishment baseline and the peer-to-peer punishment regime. When both delegated and peer-to-peer punishment are available, subjects overwhelmingly choose to implement the delegated mechanism, which then crowds out peer punishment and further increases efficiency. The delegated mechanism is low-cost, targets only the largest free rider, and is effective at deterring free riding. The efficiency gains are robust across different baseline conditions (with or without peer punishment as the initial regime).

This paper provides strong, directly relevant evidence that, in a standard linear public goods game with four players and repeated rounds, enabling a delegated punishment mechanism (with a low per-person cost and a punishment that targets only the largest free rider) increases group efficiency (net earnings) substantially compared to both no-punishment and peer-to-peer punishment regimes. The efficiency gains are primarily due to a reduction in costly peer-to-peer punishment, not just increased contributions. The findings are highly informative for predicting the effect of enabling punishment in similar game designs, especially when the punishment is centralized, low-cost, and targets the worst free rider. The results are less directly informative for other forms of punishment (e.g., peer-to-peer only, or high-cost/low-impact punishment), but the contrast with peer-to-peer punishment is explicitly tested and shows delegated punishment is superior for efficiency.

column1: The paper finds that introducing opportunities for emotion venting in a standard public goods game with punishment can reduce excessive punishment and, under certain conditions, increase group efficiency (final payoffs). However, the effect is non-linear: a simple cooling-off period (moderate venting) increases efficiency relative to baseline, while more extensive venting (virtual punishment) can reduce punishment too much, leading to lower contributions and no long-run efficiency gain. Thus, moderate emotion venting (cooling-off) is most beneficial for efficiency, while too much venting can undermine the deterrence value of punishment.

In a standard 4-player, 10-round public goods game with punishment (costly to punisher, more costly to target), the authors introduce several treatments allowing for different levels of emotion venting before punishment decisions: (1) Baseline (no venting), (2) Waiting (5-min cooling-off), (3) Waiting & Emotion (cooling-off plus self-reported emotions and unsent messages), and (4) Virtual Punishment (all previous plus non-binding virtual punishment). All treatments have punishment enabled. The main findings are: (a) All venting treatments reduce the amount and frequency of costly punishment compared to baseline

column1: The paper finds that the availability of punishment (when announced) increases contributions and efficiency (average net earnings) in a one-shot public goods game. However, induced negative emotions (anger) reduce both contributions and efficiency, and increase punishment severity. The effect of punishment on efficiency is positive relative to no punishment, but the efficiency gain is smaller when subjects are angry due to harsher and more frequent punishment.

This study uses a one-shot voluntary contributions mechanism (VCM) public goods game with and without punishment, manipulating both the announcement of punishment and participants' emotional state (anger vs. happiness). The main findings are: (1) Announcing the punishment stage increases contributions and average net earnings, confirming that punishment can improve efficiency in the short run. (2) Induced anger reduces contributions and increases the severity of punishment, leading to lower average net earnings (i.e., lower efficiency) compared to the happy condition. (3) The efficiency benefit of punishment is present but is diminished when subjects are angry, as harsher punishment increases costs and reduces net group payoffs. (4) The effect of punishment on efficiency is measured directly via average net earnings, and the design allows for clean causal inference due to the one-shot structure and between-subjects manipulation.

This paper provides direct evidence that, in a one-shot, three-player VCM with punishment, the introduction of a punishment stage (when announced) increases group efficiency (average net earnings) compared to the same game without punishment. The magnitude of the efficiency gain depends on the emotional state of participants: it is larger when subjects are happy and smaller (but still positive) when subjects are angry, due to increased punishment costs. The game design dimensions (player count, MPCR, punishment cost/tech, no chat, continuous contributions, etc.) are all clearly specified, making this study highly informative for predicting the efficiency effect of punishment in similar lab settings. The results suggest that, controlling for baseline efficiency, enabling punishment will generally increase efficiency, but the effect can be moderated by factors (such as mood) that affect the severity and frequency of punishment.

column1: The paper studies a public goods game with endogenous institution choice between decentralized punishment (DecPun), centralized punishment (CenPun), and no punishment (NoPun), under varying levels of information accuracy about others' contributions. Both punishment institutions increase efficiency (average profit) relative to no punishment, but the effect size and which institution is more efficient depend on the information environment. DecPun yields the highest efficiency under perfect information, but as information becomes noisy, the efficiency advantage of DecPun over CenPun disappears, and both are only marginally better than NoPun under high noise. The popularity and efficiency of CenPun increase when the authority avoids punishing cooperators, especially under imperfect information.

The experiment demonstrates that the efficiency gains from punishment in public goods games depend strongly on the information environment and the type of punishment institution. Under perfect information, decentralized punishment leads to the highest contributions and profits (efficiency), outperforming centralized punishment and no punishment. As information becomes less accurate (signals about others' contributions are noisy), both contributions and profits decline in all institutions, but especially in DecPun. Under moderate noise, CenPun can attract more citizens and sometimes matches or slightly exceeds DecPun in efficiency, provided the authority avoids punishing cooperators. Under high noise, neither punishment institution yields substantial efficiency gains over no punishment. The key moderator is the extent to which punishment is misapplied to cooperators, which is more likely in DecPun under noise. The paper provides direct evidence on how efficiency changes with punishment enabled versus disabled, across different institutional and informational settings.

This paper provides strong evidence that the efficiency effect of enabling punishment in public goods games is highly sensitive to the information environment and the punishment institution's design. If the control (no punishment) efficiency is low, enabling punishment (especially decentralized) can substantially increase efficiency under perfect information. However, as information becomes noisy, the efficiency gain from punishment is reduced, and the difference between decentralized and centralized punishment narrows. The presence of a central authority who avoids punishing cooperators can maintain or improve efficiency under moderate noise, but not under high noise. For prediction, the paper suggests that the marginal per-capita return, punishment cost/tech, and especially the information structure (accuracy of contribution signals) are critical moderators. The results also imply that the effect of punishment on efficiency is not uniform: it can be positive, neutral, or even negative depending on these dimensions.

column1: This laboratory experiment studies four-player public goods games with peer punishment, focusing on how the structure of the punishment network (complete vs. three types of incomplete networks) and heterogeneity in marginal per-capita return (MPCR) affect cooperation, punishment, and efficiency. The main finding is that incomplete punishment networks (especially circle and homo-pairwise) yield significantly higher group contributions and efficiency than the complete punishment network. The complete punishment network, despite allowing more potential punishers, results in lower contributions and lower efficiency, possibly due to a bystander effect reducing punishment severity. Efficiency is measured as group payoff relative to the maximum possible. The study provides direct evidence that the structure of the punishment network moderates the effect of punishment on efficiency.

The experiment finds that, in a four-player public goods game with heterogeneous MPCRs (0.3 and 0.7), incomplete punishment networks (circle and homo-pairwise) lead to higher group contributions and higher efficiency (group payoff) than the complete punishment network. The complete punishment network, despite more potential punishers, results in lower contributions and lower efficiency, likely due to a bystander effect that reduces punishment severity. The group payoff (efficiency) is lowest in the complete punishment network (86.13 out of 160), and higher in the circle (94.81), homo-pairwise (95.39), and hetero-pairwise (92.01) networks. The structure of the punishment network thus significantly moderates the effect of punishment on efficiency. The study also finds that high-MPCR individuals contribute more than low-MPCR individuals, and that punishment severity is lower in the complete network. Antisocial punishment is present in all network types.

This paper provides direct, high-quality evidence that the structure of the punishment network (i.e., who can punish whom) is a critical moderator of the effect of punishment on efficiency in public goods games with heterogeneous MPCRs. Specifically, enabling punishment by all (complete network) does not maximize efficiency
column2: instead, certain incomplete networks (circle, homo-pairwise) yield higher efficiency. For prediction tasks, this suggests that the 'punishment_tech' and the network structure (not just the presence of punishment) must be considered: more potential punishers do not always increase efficiency, and may even reduce it. The control efficiency (without punishment) is not directly reported, but the relative efficiency across punishment network types with punishment enabled is clear. The findings are directly relevant for predicting treatment efficiency as a function of punishment network structure and game design dimensions.

In a repeated public goods game with four players over ten rounds, the authors compare four conditions: no punishment, observed punishment only, unobserved (delayed) punishment only, and both punishment channels available. Both observed and unobserved punishment alone increase contributions but do not improve efficiency (average payoff) compared to the no-punishment baseline, due to the costliness of punishment. However, when both punishment channels are available, group efficiency is significantly higher than in all other conditions. This is because the threat of unobserved punishment increases the effectiveness of observed punishment, leading to higher cooperation with less punishment expenditure. The combination of punishment channels thus overcomes the typical efficiency losses seen in standard lab PGG punishment treatments.

This paper provides strong evidence that the efficiency impact of punishment in public goods games depends critically on the punishment institution. Standard punishment (observed or unobserved alone) does not improve efficiency over the control, but the combination of both channels leads to a large positive effect. For prediction, this means that the presence of multiple punishment channels (observed and unobserved) is a key moderator: if only one is present, efficiency is not improved

column1: This lab experiment finds that in a repeated public goods game with fixed groups, fixed identities, and full information, the availability of peer punishment (even when costly and inefficient) leads to much higher group earnings and cooperation compared to no-punishment controls. However, when one participant is immune from punishment, that individual free-rides, reducing group earnings. The threat of punishment, rather than its actual use, appears sufficient to sustain high efficiency in information-rich, accountable environments.

The study demonstrates that enabling peer punishment in a repeated public goods game with full information and fixed groups results in high cooperation and group earnings, even when punishment is costly (1:1 cost:impact ratio). All punishment treatments (cost-free, costly, asymmetric cost, and asymmetric immunity) yield significantly higher group earnings than the no-punishment control. However, when a group member is immune from punishment, that individual contributes less, and group earnings are reduced relative to other punishment treatments. The actual use of punishment is low, and antisocial punishment is rare, likely due to the high visibility of all actions and the possibility of long-term retaliation. The results suggest that the mere threat of punishment, in a context where all can be held accountable, is sufficient to maintain high efficiency, even if punishment is not cost-effective. The exception is when immunity allows a powerful individual to exploit the group, reducing efficiency.

This paper provides strong evidence that, in repeated public goods games with fixed groups, fixed identities, and full information about others' actions, enabling peer punishment (even if costly and inefficient) substantially increases group efficiency compared to no-punishment controls. The effect is robust across symmetric and asymmetric punishment cost structures, as long as all players are subject to punishment. However, if any player is immune from punishment, group efficiency drops due to free-riding by the immune individual. For prediction tasks, this suggests that the presence of punishment, full information, and universal accountability are key moderators of positive efficiency effects, and that the cost-effectiveness of punishment is less important in such settings. Control efficiency (no-punishment) is a strong baseline, but the addition of punishment in this design predicts a large positive shift in efficiency, unless immunity is present.

column1: The paper finds that adding a punishment stage to a repeated public goods game (in both 'maintenance' and 'provision' variants) leads to a large and significant increase in the effective size of the public good, i.e., group efficiency. Without punishment, efficiency is substantially lower in both variants, especially in the 'maintenance' condition. With punishment, efficiency rises to similar high levels in both conditions, indicating that punishment is highly effective at increasing group payoff and overcoming the decay in cooperation.

Across four lab experiments, the authors compare public goods games where the group must either maintain an existing public good (maintenance) or create one from scratch (provision). Without punishment, cooperation and efficiency are systematically lower in maintenance than provision, despite identical incentives. When a costly punishment option is introduced (partners with punishment), both maintenance and provision games see a dramatic increase in the effective size of the public good, with efficiency rising to near-optimal levels and no significant difference between the two conditions. The punishment mechanism allows each player to assign up to five punishment points to each other, costing 1 MU per point and reducing the target's earnings by 3 MU per point. The paper also finds that negative reciprocity (punishment in response to low contributions) is stronger in maintenance than provision, and that the response to being punished (increased cooperation) is also stronger in maintenance. Overall, punishment is highly effective at restoring efficiency in both types of public goods dilemmas.

This paper provides strong evidence that, in a standard linear public goods game with four players, 27 rounds, and a punishment stage (cost 1 MU, impact 3 MU), the introduction of punishment increases group efficiency from low levels (especially in maintenance) to high levels, nearly matching the social optimum. The effect is robust across both 'maintenance' and 'provision' variants, and the punishment mechanism is highly effective at overcoming the decay in cooperation seen without punishment. For prediction tasks, this paper supports the expectation that enabling punishment in similar lab PGG designs will substantially increase efficiency, regardless of whether the dilemma is framed as maintenance or provision. The specific punishment technology (cost/impact) and the absence of communication or rewards are important contextual features.

column1: The paper experimentally studies public goods games with a pool punishment system, focusing on whether prioritizing punishment of second-order free riders (those who do not support the punishment system) versus first-order free riders (those who do not contribute to the public good) affects cooperation and group efficiency. The main finding is that prioritizing second-order punishment (2To1) increases cooperation and support for the punishment system when punishment resources are scarce (low punishment ratio), but does not increase group profit (efficiency) due to high punishment costs. When punishment resources are abundant (high punishment ratio), the priority of punishment does not affect cooperation or efficiency. Thus, the effect of punishment on efficiency is context-dependent and can be positive for cooperation but not necessarily for group payoff.

The study finds that in a repeated public goods game with a pool punishment system, prioritizing second-order punishment (punishing non-supporters before non-cooperators) leads to higher cooperation and more support for the punishment system when punishment resources are scarce (PR=1). However, this does not translate into higher group profit (efficiency), as the cost of maintaining high cooperation through punishment is high. When punishment resources are abundant (PR=3), both prioritization schemes (2To1 and 1To2) achieve high cooperation and support, and there is no significant difference in group profit between them. The presence of second-order punishment (regardless of priority) is critical for achieving high cooperation, but the efficiency gains are limited by the costliness of punishment. The system's surplus (unused punishment resources) is higher when second-order punishment is prioritized.

This paper provides direct evidence that the effect of enabling punishment on efficiency in public goods games depends on the structure of the punishment system and the abundance of punishment resources. When punishment resources are scarce, prioritizing second-order punishment increases cooperation but does not improve efficiency due to high punishment costs. When resources are abundant, the priority does not matter, and both systems achieve high cooperation and similar efficiency. For prediction tasks, this suggests that the efficiency impact of punishment depends on both the punishment resource multiplier (punishment tech) and the priority rule. Control efficiency (without punishment) is not directly reported, but the results show that punishment can increase cooperation but may not always increase efficiency, especially if punishment is costly.

column1: Voluntary centralisation of punishment power (via power transfer) in a public goods game leads to higher group earnings and efficiency compared to both standard peer punishment (fixed, decentralised) and exogenously imposed centralisation. Only when group members can voluntarily delegate punishment power to willing punishers does cooperation and group welfare approach the social optimum. Decentralised peer punishment and exogenous centralisation do not sustain cooperation or efficiency.

The study introduces a 'power transfer game'—a repeated public goods game with punishment, where group members can voluntarily transfer their punishment power to others. In groups of five, three conditions were compared: (1) endogenous (voluntary) power transfer, (2) exogenous (mirrored, but not voluntary) power transfer, and (3) fixed (no transfer, standard peer punishment). Only the endogenous condition, where group members could choose whom to empower, led to sustained or increasing cooperation and higher group earnings, approaching the social optimum. In the fixed and exogenous conditions, cooperation and group earnings declined over time. The mechanism works because non-punishing cooperators delegate power to those willing to punish, and centralisation of power in the hands of pro-social punishers deters free riding. The study provides direct evidence that voluntary centralisation of punishment power can efficiently sustain cooperation and group welfare in public goods dilemmas.

This paper provides strong evidence that, in a repeated public goods game with peer punishment, allowing voluntary centralisation of punishment power (i.e., enabling group members to transfer their punishment effectiveness to others) substantially increases group efficiency compared to standard decentralised peer punishment. The effect is not observed when centralisation is imposed exogenously. For prediction tasks, this suggests that the presence of a voluntary power transfer mechanism is a key moderator: with it, efficiency is much higher than in standard peer punishment, even when the underlying MPCR, punishment cost, and other parameters are held constant. The findings are directly relevant for predicting treatment efficiency in games with and without voluntary centralisation of punishment power.

column1: Punishment, when available in a four-round public goods game, significantly decreased individual earnings (efficiency) compared to the control condition, despite a small positive effect on cooperation in the last two rounds. Gossip, in contrast, increased both cooperation and efficiency. When both gossip and punishment were available, gossip counteracted the negative effect of punishment on efficiency. Thus, punishment alone reduced efficiency, while gossip alone or in combination with punishment improved or restored efficiency.

This paper experimentally compares the effects of punishment and gossip on cooperation and efficiency in a four-round public goods game. Punishment (fee-to-fine ratio 1:3) did not significantly increase overall cooperation and significantly reduced individual earnings (efficiency) compared to control. Gossip (costless) increased both cooperation and efficiency. When both mechanisms were present, gossip offset the negative efficiency impact of punishment. The study also finds that gossip, but not punishment, has positive spillover effects on trust and trustworthiness in a subsequent trust game. The results suggest that punishment, at moderate cost, is less efficient than gossip for promoting cooperation, and that gossip can mitigate the efficiency losses from punishment.

The negative effect is robust, and the presence of a costless gossip mechanism can counteract this loss. The findings are directly relevant for predicting the efficiency impact of punishment in similar PGG designs, especially when punishment is moderately costly and anonymous. The results also suggest that the efficiency cost of punishment is not offset by increased cooperation, except possibly in the final rounds, and that gossip is a more efficient mechanism for promoting cooperation.

column1: Introducing a punishment mechanism (via a randomly assigned, anonymous monitor who can punish at a cost) in a one-shot public good game with public sector employees increases group efficiency/payoff compared to the standard public good game. The monitor game yields higher average group outcomes than the control (standard) game, and also higher than the threshold (common goal) game, due to the risk of losing all contributions in the threshold game when the threshold is not met.

The experiment compared three public good game variants: (1) standard, (2) threshold (group must reach a minimum contribution or all is lost), and (3) monitor (one randomly chosen, anonymous group member can punish others at a cost). Both the threshold and monitor games increased individual contributions compared to the standard game, with the threshold game increasing contributions the most. However, because about one-quarter of groups failed to meet the threshold and lost all contributions, the monitor game produced the highest average group payoff (efficiency). The punishment mechanism was effective: monitors punished in about 73% of groups, and punishment was targeted at low contributors. The effect of punishment on efficiency is robust to order effects and individual characteristics. The study provides direct evidence that introducing costly punishment in a one-shot, anonymous, five-player public good game increases group efficiency relative to the control.

This paper provides high-quality, directly relevant evidence for predicting the effect of enabling punishment on efficiency in a five-player, one-shot public good game with continuous contributions, no communication, and a known MPCR of 0.4. The monitor (punishment) treatment increased group efficiency/payoff compared to the control. The punishment mechanism involved a cost of 1 token to the punisher and a loss of 3 tokens to the punished. The design closely matches standard PGGs, and the efficiency outcome is directly reported. The findings support the prediction that, in similar settings, enabling punishment will increase efficiency relative to the control. The paper also provides comparative evidence on a threshold (common goal) mechanism, which increased contributions but did not increase group efficiency due to the risk of losing all contributions if the threshold was not met.

column1: The paper finds that enabling peer punishment in a linear public goods game with non-binding agreements leads to higher efficiency (group payoffs closer to the social optimum), especially when combined with a 'first-best' agreement (full cooperation target). Without punishment, 'second-best' agreements (minimum contribution targets) outperform first-best agreements in terms of efficiency, but with punishment, first-best agreements yield the highest efficiency. Punishment alone (without agreement) increases contributions but does not significantly increase payoffs due to punishment costs, except when combined with a first-best agreement.

This experiment demonstrates that in a 4-player, 10-round linear public goods game (MPCR=0.4), the introduction of a costly peer punishment stage substantially increases group efficiency only when paired with a universal, non-binding agreement requiring full cooperation. In the absence of punishment, agreements requiring only a minimum contribution (second-best) are more effective than full-cooperation agreements, as they are more likely to be formed and kept, leading to higher payoffs. When punishment is available, first-best agreements are more likely to be formed and complied with, and groups achieve payoffs very close to the social optimum. Punishment is used less frequently and more effectively in these settings, with little anti-social punishment. Punishment alone (without agreement) or with second-best agreements increases contributions but not payoffs, as punishment costs offset the gains. Thus, the efficiency gain from punishment is conditional on the presence of a clear, ambitious agreement.

For predicting the effect of enabling punishment on efficiency in public goods games, this paper provides strong evidence that the efficiency gain from punishment depends on the presence and type of agreement. In a standard linear PGG (n=4, 10 rounds, MPCR=0.4), adding punishment to a baseline game increases contributions but not payoffs (efficiency), unless a first-best (full cooperation) agreement is also present. In that case, efficiency increases dramatically, approaching the social optimum. Punishment is most effective when it can enforce a clear, ambitious group standard. If only a minimum contribution agreement is present, or if there is no agreement, punishment increases contributions but not efficiency. Thus, the predicted efficiency with punishment should be adjusted upward only if the game design includes both a punishment stage and a clear, universal agreement on full cooperation. Otherwise, the efficiency gain is likely to be small or negligible.

However, the structure of punishment matters: groups with a single prosocial leader empowered to punish achieve higher contributions and higher group earnings (after accounting for punishment costs) than both peer-punishment groups (where all can punish all) and groups with a proself leader. In a repeated public goods game, groups of four first played six rounds without punishment, then six rounds with punishment under one of three conditions: (1) only a prosocial leader could punish, (2) only a proself leader could punish, or (3) all members could punish (peer-punishment). Peer-punishment groups experienced much higher punishment costs, leading to lower overall efficiency (group earnings) than prosocial-led groups, and even lower than proself-led groups. The influence of the leader's contribution behavior on the rest of the group was a key mechanism. The study demonstrates that the design of the punishment institution (centralized vs. peer) and the social value orientation of the leader are critical moderators of punishment's effect on efficiency.

If the leader is proself, efficiency gains are limited. Both punishment conditions led to significantly higher and more stable contributions than the control. The one-punisher regime avoids redundant punishment costs, making it more efficient. The punishment mechanism used a 1:3 cost-to-impact ratio. The study provides direct evidence that both diffuse and designated punishment can sustain cooperation and efficiency, but a single punisher can do so more efficiently.

Furthermore, a single designated punisher is as effective as allowing all members to punish in sustaining cooperation, but is more efficient due to lower aggregate punishment costs. For prediction, this suggests that, under similar game parameters (player count, rounds, MPCR, punishment cost/tech), enabling punishment will increase efficiency, and that the structure of the punishment regime (single vs. diffuse) can moderate the efficiency gains. The findings are directly relevant for predicting treatment efficiency from design dimensions and control efficiency.

column1: The paper finds that in standard public goods games without intergroup competition, costly punishment increases cooperation but does not significantly improve group efficiency (net pay-off). However, when intergroup competition is introduced, groups with punishment opportunities achieve much higher efficiency and outcompete groups without punishment. In isolated public goods games, costly punishment increases cooperation but does not significantly increase net pay-off (efficiency), as the costs of punishment offset the gains from higher contributions. When intergroup competition is introduced, groups with punishment opportunities achieve much higher contributions and net pay-offs, both in asymmetric (one group can punish, one cannot) and symmetric (both can punish) competition. In asymmetric competition, the efficiency benefit is dramatic: even the lowest-earning individual in the punishment group outperforms the highest in the no-punishment group. In symmetric competition, the efficiency benefit is positive but smaller and only marginally significant. Punishment also reduces within-group inequality in pay-offs. The paper concludes that intergroup competition is a key moderator of the efficiency effects of costly punishment.

This paper provides strong evidence that the effect of punishment on efficiency in public goods games depends critically on whether there is intergroup competition. In the absence of group competition, enabling punishment does not reliably increase efficiency. With group competition, punishment can substantially increase efficiency, especially when only some groups have access to punishment. The design dimensions most relevant for prediction are the presence of group competition, punishment cost and effectiveness, group size (8), number of rounds (30), and the absence of communication or reputation mechanisms. The control efficiency (no punishment) is much lower than the treatment efficiency (with punishment) in the presence of group competition, but not in isolated groups. column1: The paper finds that the effect of punishment on efficiency depends on group size and the punishment institution. In small groups (n=4), anonymous punishment (AP) increases efficiency more than public punisher ID (PPID) or no-punishment (VCM). In larger groups (n=8, 12), PPID increases efficiency more than AP or VCM, and AP can even reduce efficiency below the no-punishment baseline. The legitimacy of punishment (as perceived by the punished, especially when multiple group members punish or when punisher identity is known) is key to whether punishment increases cooperation and efficiency.

This paper experimentally compares three public goods game treatments: (1) standard voluntary contribution mechanism (VCM, no punishment), (2) VCM with anonymous punishment (AP), and (3) VCM with public punisher ID to the punished (PPID). Group sizes are 4, 8, and 12. In all treatments, subjects choose continuous contributions from 0 to 10, and in punishment treatments, each subject can punish one other group member per round, with a cost of 1 EMU to reduce the target's payoff by 2 EMUs. Communication is not allowed. Efficiency (group earnings as a percentage of the maximum possible) is reported for each treatment and group size. Key findings: (a) In small groups (n=4), AP yields the highest efficiency (85.55%), followed by PPID (78.25%) and VCM (76.60%). (b) In larger groups (n=8, 12), PPID yields the highest efficiency (80.60% and 78.05%), followed by AP (76.10% and 61.35%), with VCM lowest (68.60% and 63.30%). (c) In large groups, AP can reduce efficiency below the no-punishment baseline. (d) The number of punishers and the perceived legitimacy of punishment are critical for increasing cooperation and efficiency. (e) Punishment is more effective at increasing efficiency when it is seen as legitimate (e.g., when multiple group members punish a free-rider, or when punisher identity is known and retaliation is possible).

This paper provides direct, quantitative evidence for predicting the effect of punishment on efficiency in public goods games, conditional on group size and punishment institution. It shows that the effect of enabling punishment is not always positive: in small groups, anonymous punishment can increase efficiency more than public punishment, but in larger groups, public punishment (with punisher ID revealed) is more effective and can prevent the efficiency losses seen with anonymous punishment. The marginal per-capita return, punishment cost, and punishment effectiveness are all clearly specified, and the control (VCM) efficiency is reported for each group size. The results support the importance of group size, punishment institution (anonymity vs. identifiability), and the legitimacy of punishment as moderators of the punishment effect on efficiency. For prediction, the paper provides a table of efficiency outcomes for each treatment and group size, allowing direct mapping from design dimensions and control efficiency to treatment efficiency.

column1: The paper finds that heterogeneity in punishment effectiveness alone does not affect efficiency or cooperation compared to symmetry. Endowment heterogeneity reduces efficiency and cooperation, mainly because rich members contribute less. However, when endowment and punishment effectiveness heterogeneities are combined (joint heterogeneities), efficiency and cooperation are not reduced compared to symmetry, and are higher than under endowment heterogeneity alone. In the 'Rich strong' treatment (richest is most effective punisher), efficiency is higher than in the 'Poor strong' treatment (poorest is most effective punisher) among high-cooperation groups, due to less punishment being required to sustain cooperation.

This lab experiment uses a linear public good game with peer punishment to study the effects of heterogeneity in endowment and punishment effectiveness, both separately and jointly. The main findings are: (1) Heterogeneity in punishment effectiveness alone does not affect efficiency or cooperation compared to symmetric groups. (2) Endowment heterogeneity (rich and poor members) reduces efficiency and cooperation, as rich members contribute a lower share of their endowment. (3) When both endowment and punishment effectiveness are heterogeneous (either the rich or the poor is the most effective punisher), efficiency and cooperation are not reduced compared to symmetry, and are higher than under endowment heterogeneity alone. (4) Among groups that achieve high cooperation, efficiency is higher in the 'Rich strong' treatment (richest is most effective punisher) than in the 'Poor strong' treatment, because less punishment is needed to sustain cooperation. (5) Overall, congruent heterogeneities (richest is most effective punisher) do not hinder and may even facilitate efficiency and cooperation compared to endowment heterogeneity alone.

This paper provides strong evidence that, in linear public good games with peer punishment, the presence of punishment generally increases efficiency compared to control conditions with endowment heterogeneity alone. However, the efficiency gain from punishment is moderated by the structure of heterogeneity: punishment is most effective (in terms of efficiency) when either all players are symmetric or when the richest player is also the most effective punisher. Endowment heterogeneity without matching punishment effectiveness reduces efficiency, but joint heterogeneities (especially congruent ones) restore efficiency to levels comparable to symmetry. For prediction, this suggests that punishment will generally increase efficiency, but the magnitude of the effect depends on the alignment of endowment and punishment effectiveness. The control efficiency (without punishment) is lowest under endowment heterogeneity, and the efficiency gain from enabling punishment is largest in this case, especially if punishment effectiveness is also heterogeneous and congruent with endowment.

In the complete and star (hierarchical) networks, punishment leads to higher efficiency compared to the no-punishment baseline. In the circle and line networks, punishment increases contributions but the cost of punishment outweighs the gains, resulting in lower efficiency than the no-punishment baseline. Central players in the star network use punishment in a prosocial way and do not retaliate, leading to higher group efficiency. In contrast, antisocial punishment and retaliation are more common in the line and circle networks, undermining efficiency.

This paper provides direct evidence that the effect of punishment on efficiency in public goods games is highly sensitive to the network structure. If the game design includes a hierarchical (star) or complete network, enabling punishment is likely to increase efficiency relative to the control. In other incomplete networks (circle, line), punishment may reduce efficiency due to costly antisocial punishment and retaliation. The paper also provides detailed parameterization of the game (player count, rounds, MPCR, punishment cost/tech), making it highly informative for prediction tasks that use these dimensions. Control (VCM) and treatment (PUN) efficiency values are reported for each network, allowing for direct calibration.

column1: The paper finds that exogenously imposed mild (non-deterrent) punishment does not significantly increase efficiency or compliance in a one-shot public goods game compared to no punishment. However, when mild punishment is endogenously enacted via group voting, efficiency and compliance increase substantially—net efficiency nearly doubles compared to exogenous mild law and is about three times higher than no law. Severe (deterrent) punishment, whether exogenous or endogenous, leads to near-complete compliance and maximal efficiency. The mechanism for endogenous mild law's effectiveness is that voting for the law signals commitment and raises expectations of cooperation, activating conditional cooperation norms.

In a one-shot, linear public goods game with groups of three, the authors compare no law, exogenous mild law (non-deterrent sanction), exogenous severe law (deterrent sanction), and endogenous (voted) versions of mild and severe law. Exogenous mild law does not significantly increase efficiency or compliance compared to no law (net efficiency: 33% vs. 30%). Exogenous severe law achieves near-maximal efficiency (89%). When mild law is enacted by group vote, net efficiency rises to 62%, nearly double the exogenous mild law and about three times the no law condition. Endogenous severe law achieves 96% net efficiency. The increase in efficiency under endogenous mild law is not due to selection effects but to the causal effect of the law: voting for mild law signals commitment, raises expectations of cooperation, and activates conditional cooperation. If mild law is rejected, efficiency is even lower than in the no law condition. The results show that the effectiveness of mild punishment depends critically on whether it is self-imposed or externally imposed.

For prediction tasks, the presence of endogenous (voted) mild punishment should be expected to yield much higher efficiency than exogenous mild punishment, even when the punishment is non-deterrent. Severe punishment (deterrent) is highly effective regardless of endogeneity. The game is one-shot, with no communication, group size of 3, and a marginal per-capita return of 0.5. The findings are directly relevant for predicting efficiency outcomes in similar lab PGGs with and without punishment, especially when considering the mode of law enactment (voted vs. imposed).

column1: The paper finds that decentralized punishment increases contributions and efficiency in standard (normal) public goods games, but is much less effective in privileged groups (where one member has a higher marginal return). In normal groups, punishment increases both contributions and group earnings, especially in later rounds. In privileged groups, punishment increases contributions and earnings only slightly, and it significantly increases inequality. Thus, the effect of punishment on efficiency is positive in normal groups but weak or negligible in privileged groups.

This experiment compares standard (normal) and privileged public goods groups, with and without the option for decentralized costly punishment. In normal groups (all members have the same marginal per-capita return), punishment substantially increases contributions and group earnings, especially in later rounds. In privileged groups (one member has a high marginal return, others low), punishment increases contributions and earnings only slightly, and it increases inequality. The main reason is that punishment is less targeted and less effective in privileged groups: high-benefit members punish in an unstructured way, and low-benefit members respond weakly to punishment. As a result, the efficiency gains from punishment are much smaller in privileged groups than in normal groups.

This paper provides direct evidence that the effect of punishment on efficiency depends strongly on group composition, specifically on whether the group is homogeneous (normal) or contains privileged members (heterogeneous marginal returns). For standard linear PGGs with 3 players, 10 rounds, no chat, continuous contributions, and known MPCR, punishment increases efficiency, especially in later rounds. However, if the group is privileged (one high-benefit, two low-benefit), the efficiency gain from punishment is much smaller, and inequality increases. Thus, when predicting the effect of punishment on efficiency, it is crucial to account for heterogeneity in marginal returns. Control efficiency (without punishment) is higher in privileged groups, but the treatment effect of punishment is much weaker than in normal groups.

column1: The paper finds that combining material punishment with norm-signaling (sanction treatment) leads to higher and more stable cooperation and, crucially, to higher group efficiency (average net earnings) than either punishment or norm-signaling alone. The sanction treatment achieves higher payoffs due to both increased cooperation and reduced punishment costs, overcoming the typical efficiency losses seen when punishment is used in isolation.

In a repeated public goods game with 4-person groups over 30 rounds, the study compares three treatments: (1) punishment only, (2) norm-signaling (message) only, and (3) both punishment and norm-signaling (sanction). In the critical rounds where treatments differ (rounds 11-20), the sanction treatment yields significantly higher average net earnings (31% higher than punishment, 16% higher than message) and higher contributions, with less frequent and less intense punishment. The efficiency gains in the sanction treatment are attributed to the combination of explicit norm communication and the credible threat of punishment, which together increase norm salience and reduce the need for costly punishment. The findings are robust in both human experiments and agent-based simulations.

This paper provides strong evidence that, in a standard linear public goods game with costly punishment, the addition of norm-signaling (explicit communication of normative expectations) to punishment substantially increases group efficiency compared to punishment alone. The efficiency gains are due to both higher cooperation and lower punishment costs. For prediction tasks, this suggests that the presence of norm-signaling or communication channels that make norms salient can be a critical moderator of punishment's effect on efficiency. The game design dimensions most relevant here are the presence of punishment, the ability to send norm-signaling messages, and the structure of feedback about others' actions. The control efficiency (without punishment or norm-signaling) is lower than in the combined treatment. The results imply that, all else equal, enabling both punishment and norm-signaling will yield higher efficiency than enabling punishment alone.

column1: The paper reports that introducing punishment in a standard linear public goods game (VCM) in Southern Europe does not reliably increase efficiency, due to high levels of antisocial punishment. In contrast, introducing punishment in a weakest-link mechanism (WLM) public goods game (where group output is determined by the minimum contribution) leads to large and significant efficiency gains, with most groups earning more with punishment than without. The difference is attributed to much lower levels of antisocial punishment in the WLM compared to the VCM.

In a lab experiment in Spain, groups of four played two types of public goods games: a standard linear VCM and a weakest-link minimum game (WLM), each for 20 rounds without punishment and then 20 rounds with punishment. In the VCM, punishment led to only moderate increases in public good provision and did not increase group efficiency, due to substantial antisocial punishment (punishing high contributors). In the WLM, punishment led to a dramatic increase in public good provision and group efficiency, with antisocial punishment being rare and most groups earning more with punishment than without. The effectiveness of punishment in raising efficiency is thus highly dependent on the production technology of the public good, with complementarity (WLM) supporting positive effects of punishment even in a culture with high antisocial punishment in linear games.

This paper provides strong evidence that the effect of punishment on efficiency in public goods games is highly sensitive to the production function: in linear VCMs, punishment may not improve efficiency in cultures with high antisocial punishment, but in weakest-link (complementary) games, punishment can substantially increase efficiency. For prediction, the game structure (linear vs. weakest-link) is a critical moderator. Control efficiency (without punishment) is similar across games, but the treatment effect of punishment is much more positive in the WLM. The paper also provides parameter values for player count, rounds, MPCR, punishment cost/tech, and information structure, which can be used to inform predictions in similar designs.

column1: The paper finds that, controlling for average punishment effectiveness, asymmetric punishment institutions (where one player has higher punishment effectiveness than others) are as effective and as efficient as symmetric punishment institutions in public goods games. There is no significant difference in group earnings (efficiency) between symmetric and asymmetric punishment institutions. Higher average punishment effectiveness increases contributions, but does not significantly affect average earnings. Strong (high-effectiveness) players earn more than weak players, but this does not affect group-level efficiency.

This laboratory experiment compares symmetric and asymmetric punishment institutions in a standard public goods game with punishment. Asymmetry is introduced by giving one player higher punishment effectiveness (impact per unit cost) than the other three. The main findings are: (1) Asymmetric punishment institutions are as effective as symmetric ones in sustaining cooperation and efficiency, as measured by group earnings. (2) There is no significant difference in efficiency (group earnings) between symmetric and asymmetric punishment institutions, controlling for average punishment effectiveness. (3) Higher average punishment effectiveness increases contributions, but does not significantly increase efficiency. (4) Strong players (with higher punishment effectiveness) punish more and earn more than weak players, but do not contribute less. (5) The behavioral regularities of symmetric punishment institutions (e.g., punishment targeting free riders, response to punishment) carry over to asymmetric institutions.

This paper provides strong evidence that, in public goods games with punishment, the presence of asymmetry in punishment effectiveness (i.e., one player can punish more effectively than others) does not significantly affect group efficiency compared to symmetric punishment, as long as average punishment effectiveness is held constant. Thus, for the prediction task, the efficiency effect of enabling punishment should be predicted primarily based on the average punishment effectiveness, not on whether punishment power is symmetric or asymmetric. The paper also confirms that higher average punishment effectiveness increases contributions, but this does not necessarily translate into higher efficiency due to the costs of punishment. Control efficiency (without punishment) is not directly reported, but the main comparison is between symmetric and asymmetric punishment with the same average effectiveness.

column1: The paper synthesizes experimental evidence from public goods games and related economic games, showing that allowing costly punishment of defectors leads to higher cooperation and, crucially, to higher group payoffs and efficiency. When punishment is permitted, cooperation is sustained or increases, and group earnings rise significantly compared to control conditions without punishment. The effect is robust across different group assignment protocols and is not explained by self-interest or strategic future-oriented punishment.

Experimental public goods games consistently show that when participants can punish defectors at a personal cost, cooperation rates remain high or even increase over time, and group payoffs (efficiency) are substantially higher than when punishment is not allowed. In the Fehr & Gächter (2000) experiments, for example, allowing punishment led to a 40% increase in net payoffs to all subjects, even after accounting for the costs of punishment. The effect is observed even under strict anonymity and in one-shot or non-repeated interactions, indicating that the mechanism is not driven by expectations of future reciprocity. The paper also reviews cross-cultural evidence and evolutionary models, but the core experimental result is that punishment opportunities robustly improve group efficiency in public goods game environments.

This paper provides strong, direct evidence that enabling costly punishment in public goods games increases group efficiency relative to control conditions without punishment. The effect is robust across standard lab PGG designs with 4 players, 10 rounds, no chat, continuous contributions, and known MPCR. The magnitude of the efficiency gain is substantial (e.g., 40% increase in net payoffs in Fehr & Gächter 2000). The findings are directly relevant for predicting the effect of punishment on efficiency given the control game design and efficiency, especially in standard PGG settings. The paper also discusses the importance of group structure (e.g., partner vs. stranger matching), but the positive effect of punishment on efficiency is consistent across these variations.

column1: The paper reviews and synthesizes a range of experimental studies on public goods games, focusing on the effects of punishment, endogenous institution choice, and reputation mechanisms. It finds that while punishment reliably increases cooperation and contributions, it often reduces efficiency and group payoffs in short or standard-length games due to the costliness of punishment. However, in longer time horizons or when combined with reputation mechanisms, punishment can lead to higher efficiency and group payoffs. The endogenous choice of sanctioning institutions (voting with one's feet) leads to the predominance of punishment institutions and high cooperation, but efficiency gains depend on the time horizon and the interaction with other mechanisms (e.g., reputation). The effect of punishment on efficiency is thus context-dependent: often negative in short games, but potentially positive in long or reputation-rich environments.

Punishment opportunities in public goods games increase cooperation and contributions, but typically reduce efficiency and group payoffs in standard (short) experimental settings due to the destruction of resources through costly punishment. In most experiments with 10 or fewer rounds, average payoffs are lower with punishment than without. However, in longer games (e.g., 50 rounds), or when punishment is combined with effective reputation mechanisms, efficiency can be higher with punishment. Endogenous institution choice leads most participants to eventually select punishment institutions, which then sustain high cooperation, but efficiency gains are not guaranteed unless the time horizon is long or reputation is leveraged. The effect of punishment on efficiency is thus mixed and highly sensitive to game design dimensions such as number of rounds and the presence of reputation mechanisms.

This paper provides strong evidence that the effect of enabling punishment on efficiency in public goods games is not universally positive or negative, but depends critically on the number of rounds (time horizon) and the presence of reputation or endogenous institution choice. For standard short games (10 rounds or fewer), enabling punishment is likely to reduce efficiency relative to control. For longer games (e.g., 50 rounds), or when combined with reputation mechanisms, punishment can increase efficiency. The paper also highlights the importance of endogenous institution choice, which can foster high cooperation and, under the right conditions, higher efficiency. When predicting treatment efficiency from game design, the number of rounds and the presence of reputation or endogenous choice mechanisms are key moderators.

column1: The paper finds that introducing punishment opportunities in a public goods game can increase or decrease efficiency depending on the structure of the punishment system. A single round of punishment (with anonymity for punishers) increases contributions and welfare relative to no punishment. However, when counterpunishment (the ability to punish punishers) is possible, contributions and welfare decrease, sometimes below the level with no punishment at all. Allowing sanction enforcement (punishing those who fail to punish free riders) has a small positive effect on contributions, but this is outweighed by the negative effect of counterpunishment. Multiple rounds of punishment (as in the six-stage treatment) further reduce both contributions and welfare, with welfare falling below the no-punishment baseline.

The experiment demonstrates that the effect of punishment on efficiency in public goods games is highly sensitive to the design of the punishment mechanism. In the Baseline (single-stage punishment) treatment, efficiency is high: contributions and earnings are close to the social optimum. When a second stage of punishment is added and counterpunishment is possible, contributions and welfare fall significantly. The positive effect of sanction enforcement (punishing those who fail to punish free riders) is present but smaller than the negative effect of counterpunishment. In the most extreme case, with five rounds of punishment (6SFI), both contributions and welfare are significantly lower than in the Baseline, and welfare is even lower than in the no-punishment scenario. The results show that punishment can backfire and reduce efficiency if it enables cycles of retaliation (counterpunishment) or is too unconstrained.

This paper provides strong evidence that the efficiency gains from enabling punishment in public goods games depend critically on the details of the punishment system. If punishment is anonymous and limited to a single round, it increases efficiency. If counterpunishment is possible, or if there are multiple rounds of punishment, efficiency can decrease, sometimes below the no-punishment baseline. For prediction, the presence of counterpunishment opportunities, the number of punishment rounds, and the information structure (anonymity of punishers) are key moderators. Control efficiency (without punishment) is high in this design, and adding punishment can either increase or decrease efficiency depending on these moderators.
