column1: This paper studies the effect of enabling costly reward and/or punishment options for responders in a repeated ultimatum bargaining game. Efficiency (aggregate payoff) is highest when both reward and punishment are available (UPR), lowest when only reward is available (UR), and intermediate in the baseline (U) and punishment-only (UP) treatments. The presence of punishment (alone or with reward) increases acceptance of low offers and can increase efficiency in environments with low offers, but the presence of reward alone reduces offers and efficiency. The effects are asymmetric and depend on the combination of instruments available.

The experiment finds that adding costly punishment and/or reward options for responders in ultimatum bargaining changes both proposer and responder behavior. When only reward is available, proposers make lower offers and efficiency drops. When only punishment is available, acceptance of low offers increases, and efficiency for low offers is higher than baseline. When both reward and punishment are available, both offers and efficiency are highest. The use of reward and punishment is rare and mostly symbolic, so efficiency losses from their direct use are minimal. The main efficiency effects come from changes in offer and acceptance behavior, not from the direct cost of sanctions. The results suggest that punishment options can increase efficiency in settings with low offers, while reward options alone may reduce efficiency.

This paper provides direct evidence on how the availability and cost/effectiveness of punishment and reward options affect efficiency in a two-player bargaining environment. While not a public goods game, the findings are relevant for predicting efficiency effects of punishment in asymmetric, bilateral settings with costly sanctions. The results show that costly punishment (with 1:1 cost-impact ratio) can increase efficiency by increasing acceptance of low offers, especially when offers are low, but that reward alone can reduce efficiency. The combination of both instruments yields the highest efficiency. For prediction tasks, the paper suggests that the effect of punishment on efficiency depends on the presence of reward, the cost/effectiveness of punishment, and the baseline offer/acceptance norms. The findings are most transferable to settings with costly, direct, one-to-one punishment and reward, and less so to multiplayer or public goods environments.

column1: The paper studies a linear public goods game with and without communication and with homogeneous or heterogeneous returns. All treatments allow costly rewards (not punishment). Communication strongly increases efficiency (group earnings) in both homogeneous and heterogeneous groups, but the effect is much larger in homogeneous groups. Allowing communication and rewards in a public goods game leads to near-maximal efficiency in homogeneous groups, but only partial efficiency in heterogeneous groups where returns from the public good differ. In homogeneous groups, communication increases group earnings to 94% of the maximum, while in heterogeneous groups, the increase is only 80% of the maximum. The main reason is that most heterogeneous groups prioritize equality or compromise between equality and efficiency, rather than maximizing group earnings. Rewards are not systematically used to offset inequality. The loss in efficiency in heterogeneous groups is due both to lower contributions and to under-use of rewards. The study demonstrates that normative conflict can limit the effectiveness of self-governance mechanisms in promoting efficiency in heterogeneous populations.

For prediction tasks, this suggests that the presence of heterogeneity in returns (mpcr differences) is a strong moderator that limits the efficiency benefit of enabling communication and rewards. column1: Introducing an intermediary institution that enforces punishment (ENFO) for cheating in a repeated, optional prisoner's dilemma with random matching significantly increases efficiency (average payoffs) compared to a baseline with no intermediary. The INFO institution's effect is limited, in part because reputation can be quickly repaired and there is no centralized punishment. The study also finds that the cost to use INFO reduces its adoption and thus its effectiveness. Over time, ENFO treatments move toward higher efficiency, while INFO treatments tend to regress toward less efficient outcomes.

The study provides direct evidence that targeted punishment can sustain high-efficiency collusion even in large groups, contrary to standard theory and previous experimental results without punishment.

column1: Introducing punishment in the market experiment significantly increases welfare (average earnings) compared to the market baseline without punishment. The punishment mechanism leads to higher socially responsible behavior (more fair product purchases), reduces anti-social retaliation (money burning), and results in higher group payoffs. Religious priming has a weaker and less robust effect on welfare. The market baseline (no punishment) yields lower efficiency than the punishment treatment.

The study uses a lab-in-the-field market experiment in Ethiopia to test the effects of punishment and religious priming on socially responsible behavior and welfare. In the market baseline (no punishment), only about 21% of purchases are fair (no negative externality), and average earnings are about 56 Birr. When punishment is introduced (observers can punish at a cost of 1 Birr to reduce others' earnings by 5 Birr), the proportion of fair purchases rises to 95%, and average earnings increase to 66 Birr. Punishment also reduces anti-social behavior in a subsequent joy-of-destruction game (money burning). Religious priming increases fair purchases to 32% but does not significantly improve welfare compared to the baseline. The results show that punishment mechanisms are highly effective at increasing efficiency (group welfare) in this market context.

This paper provides strong evidence that, in a market game with negative externalities, adding a punishment mechanism (with a cost of 1 to reduce another's payoff by 5) substantially increases efficiency (average group earnings) compared to a baseline with no punishment. The effect is large and robust. The design is not a standard PGG but is adjacent: it is a market/trade game with externalities and third parties, and the efficiency measure is directly comparable (average earnings relative to maximum possible). The punishment mechanism is costly and effective. Religious priming has a much weaker effect. For prediction tasks, this paper supports the expectation that, in similar market or externality games, enabling punishment with a moderate cost-to-impact ratio will lead to a large increase in efficiency over the control. The effect is much larger than that of non-monetary priming.

column1: The paper finds that collective (pool) punishment in a common-pool resource (CPR) game only sometimes improves resource conservation and group payoffs, and that adding second-order punishment (punishing tax evaders) actually reduces efficiency and increases resource exhaustion. The effect of punishment on efficiency is highly heterogeneous: in some groups, collective punishment helps conserve resources, but in others it does not. Second-order punishment leads to higher extraction as subjects compensate for tax costs, resulting in lower payoffs and more frequent resource collapse.

In a repeated CPR lab experiment with three-person groups, the introduction of collective (pool) punishment (10P) does not significantly improve efficiency or payoffs compared to the baseline without punishment. Only a minority of groups in the 10P treatment maintain higher resource levels and payoffs. When second-order punishment (20P) is added (punishing both over-harvesters and tax evaders), the sanctioning institution persists, but efficiency and payoffs decline: subjects extract more to compensate for tax costs, and resource exhaustion becomes more frequent. The effect of punishment is thus context-dependent: collective punishment can promote conservation in some groups, but second-order punishment undermines efficiency overall. The paper provides direct evidence on group payoffs, resource exhaustion, and the mechanisms by which punishment affects behavior.

This paper provides direct evidence that the effect of punishment on efficiency in CPR-like environments is not uniformly positive and depends on the institutional design. Pool punishment (collective, voluntary tax-funded) does not reliably increase efficiency compared to no punishment, and second-order punishment (punishing tax evaders) can reduce efficiency by increasing extraction and resource collapse. For prediction, the presence of second-order punishment is a strong negative moderator for efficiency, while voluntary collective punishment has a mixed or null effect. The findings suggest that simply enabling punishment is not sufficient to guarantee higher efficiency

column1: Introducing weak external enforcement or local monitoring (with sanctions for poaching) in a dynamic common-pool resource game with communication among insiders leads to higher group earnings and more sustainable resource use compared to a poaching-only (no enforcement) condition. However, neither enforcement regime achieves full deterrence or the cooperative optimum, and combining external and local monitoring does not further improve efficiency. The main effect of punishment is to partially restore efficiency lost to poaching.

The paper finds that in a dynamic common-pool resource game with insiders (who can communicate) and outsiders (who cannot), the introduction of poaching without monitoring or sanctions dramatically reduces insiders' earnings and resource sustainability, nearly eliminating the efficiency gains from cooperation. Adding weak external enforcement (low-probability monitoring and fines) or allowing insiders to invest in monitoring (with the same fine) both significantly reduce poaching and increase insiders' earnings and harvests, but do not fully restore efficiency to baseline (no-poaching) levels. Combining external and local monitoring does not further reduce poaching or increase efficiency. The main constraint is insiders' inability to coordinate sufficient monitoring investment. The results are robust across field (TURF members) and student samples.

This paper provides direct evidence that, in a dynamic CPR game with communication among insiders, the introduction of punishment (via monitoring and fines for poaching) increases group efficiency relative to a poaching-only control, but the effect is partial and depends on the ability to coordinate monitoring. The effect is similar whether monitoring is provided externally or by insiders, and combining both does not yield additional efficiency. For prediction, the presence of punishment (even if weak) should be expected to increase efficiency above the poaching-only baseline, but not to the level of the no-poaching or full-cooperation baseline. The magnitude of the effect is limited by the monitoring probability and the coordination of monitoring investment.

Instead, punishment is associated with lower group payoffs due to retaliation cycles and reduced cooperation. In all games, the average group benefit under punishment is lower than under individual decision-making or leadership. Leadership (especially recommending leadership) increases efficiency, while punishment governance leads to the lowest efficiency. The negative effect of punishment on efficiency is robust across games with and without monetary incentives.

column1: The paper studies a three-player game where a third party can sanction two agents who may jointly cause harm. The experiment manipulates whether the two agents have symmetric or asymmetric wealth and whether the sanctioning schedule is observable before the agents act. The main finding is that when the third party uses discriminatory sanctions (especially when wealth is asymmetric and the sanctioning schedule is observable), the agents are more likely to coordinate on an efficient outcome, avoiding mutual harm and increasing group efficiency. Thus, discriminatory punishment by a third party can enhance efficiency in this setting.

The experiment demonstrates that third-party discriminatory sanctioning (especially when preannounced and when agents differ in wealth) increases the likelihood that the two agents coordinate to avoid mutual harm, resulting in higher group efficiency. When the third party sanctions equally, agents are less likely to coordinate efficiently. The effect is robust to the order protocol (sequential vs. simultaneous), but is strongest when the sanctioning schedule is observable. Asymmetric wealth increases the tendency for the third party to sanction the richer agent more, confirming the 'deep-pocket' hypothesis. Overall, the ability to use discriminatory punishment, and to preannounce it, enables higher efficiency in this coordination dilemma.

This paper provides direct evidence that, in a coordination game adjacent to the public goods game, enabling a third party to use discriminatory punishment (especially when the punishment schedule is observable) increases group efficiency by facilitating coordination and avoiding mutual harm. The findings suggest that, in similar environments, the design dimensions of punishment observability and the ability to discriminate in punishment can be leveraged to improve efficiency. The results are most relevant for settings where a third party can precommit to a punishment schedule and where agents may differ in wealth or status. For prediction tasks, the presence of observable, flexible, and potentially discriminatory punishment is likely to increase efficiency relative to control conditions without such punishment.

column1: The paper uses a laboratory experiment with a rule-following task (street-crossing under a red light) that is structurally similar to a public goods game with negative externalities and peer punishment. The main finding is that introducing punishment (especially when combined with endogenous observability) increases norm compliance (reduces violations), but at the cost of lower total group payoffs due to the direct costs of punishment and increased inequality, particularly for minority group members. Thus, while punishment increases compliance, it reduces efficiency relative to the no-punishment baseline.

The laboratory experiment shows that the availability of peer punishment (especially when participants can choose whom to observe and punish) increases rule compliance, particularly among minority (outgroup) members who are more likely to be monitored. However, the introduction of punishment reduces total group payoffs compared to the no-punishment baseline, due to the direct costs of punishing and being punished. The highest compliance (lowest violation rate) occurs when both observability and punishment are present, but this comes with increased inequality: minorities earn significantly less than majorities or locals. The frequency of fully compliant (high-norm) groups is higher with punishment, but overall efficiency (average payoff relative to the social optimum) is lower in punishment treatments than in control. Punishment is applied non-discriminatorily, but minorities are more likely to be observed and thus punished, leading to a 'compliance minority effect' and a 'local premium' in payoffs.

For prediction tasks, this suggests that, all else equal, enabling punishment in similar designs will likely decrease average efficiency, even if compliance increases. The effect is strongest when observability is endogenous (players choose whom to monitor) and when group composition allows for minority/majority distinctions. The findings are most directly relevant to settings with peer punishment, endogenous monitoring, and negative externalities from non-cooperation.

The results suggest that costly punishment can reduce efficiency, and its effect is culturally contingent.

The results are contrasted with previous US-based studies, where costly punishment increased cooperation but did not improve group payoff. column1: The paper presents a theoretical and simulation-based analysis of a coupled socio-ecological system where agents harvest a common pool resource and can be sanctioned (ostracized) for defecting. It finds that the effectiveness of social sanction in promoting cooperation and sustaining higher resource levels (a proxy for efficiency) increases with the average number of social ties (network degree). In well-mixed or highly connected populations, social sanction is more effective, leading to higher equilibrium resource levels and more cooperation. In sparsely connected networks, defectors can cluster and evade sanction, resulting in lower cooperation and resource depletion.

The study extends a previous analytical model of social sanction (ostracism) in common pool resource extraction to populations with complex network structures. It finds that, contrary to some prior work, cooperation and resource sustainability are promoted by higher network connectivity when social sanction is present. In networks with fewer social ties, defectors can cluster and avoid sanction, leading to lower cooperation and lower equilibrium resource levels. The model shows that the equilibrium resource level (a proxy for group efficiency) is higher in well-mixed or highly connected networks, and lower in sparsely connected ones. The findings are robust across different network topologies (random, scale-free, community-structured) and network sizes.

For the downstream prediction task, this suggests that, all else equal, games with higher player connectivity or more opportunities for sanctioning will see a greater positive effect of punishment on efficiency. The paper does not provide direct experimental data, but its results are highly relevant for predicting the effect of punishment in networked or structured populations.

column1: The paper finds that the effect of 'milestone' regulation (intermediate targets with probabilistic group loss if missed) on efficiency in a cumulative threshold public goods game depends on the scenario. In a scenario with no continuous efficiency gains and low free-riding disincentives, strict milestones increase efficiency and the probability of reaching the final target. In a scenario with continuous efficiency gains and high free-riding disincentives, strict milestones reduce efficiency. In an intermediate scenario, the effects cancel out. Thus, milestones can be efficiency enhancing or detrimental depending on the underlying payoff structure and risk parameters.

This laboratory experiment tests whether adding intermediate contribution targets ('milestones') to a cumulative threshold public goods game increases efficiency, measured by group payoffs and the probability of reaching a final target. The game is played in groups of 5 over 6 rounds, with treatments varying the strictness of milestones, the marginal per-capita return (mpcr), and the probability of group loss if targets are missed. The main findings are: (1) In a scenario with no continuous efficiency gains (i.e., only reaching the target matters), strict milestones increase both contributions and the probability of reaching the target, thus enhancing efficiency. (2) In a scenario with continuous efficiency gains (i.e., contributions always increase payoffs), strict milestones actually reduce average contributions and efficiency, as groups focus on meeting milestones rather than maximizing payoffs. (3) In an intermediate scenario, the positive and negative effects cancel out. The effect of milestones is thus context-dependent, and their efficiency impact is not universally positive.

This paper provides direct evidence that the effect of punishment-like milestone mechanisms on efficiency in public-goods-like games is highly sensitive to the underlying payoff structure. When the only way to generate group payoffs is to reach a threshold (no continuous efficiency gains), strict milestones (punishment for missing intermediate targets) can improve efficiency by increasing coordination and contributions. However, when continuous efficiency gains are present (i.e., contributions always increase payoffs), strict milestones can reduce efficiency, as they may distract from maximizing group welfare. For prediction, this means that the presence and structure of milestone/punishment mechanisms, the marginal per-capita return, and the risk of group loss must all be considered. Control efficiency (without milestones/punishment) is a strong moderator: if control efficiency is already high, milestones may not help and can even hurt. The findings are directly relevant for predicting treatment efficiency from design dimensions in cumulative threshold public goods games with milestone/punishment features.

column1: In a repeated Bertrand duopoly experiment with optional communication, most subjects use graduated, proportionate punishment strategies (e.g., Tit-for-tat) rather than harsh, disproportionate punishments (e.g., Grim trigger). These softer punishment strategies are at least as profitable as harsher ones, with Tit-for-tat yielding the highest future earnings. Communication increases the likelihood of cooperative (high-price) outcomes but does not lead to more frequent use of harsh punishment strategies.

The experiment finds that the vast majority of subjects do not use harsh, disproportionate punishment strategies. Instead, most use graduated or lenient strategies, such as Tit-for-tat, which respond proportionally to deviations. Regression analysis shows that adopting Tit-for-tat leads to significantly higher present discounted value of earnings than harsher punishment strategies, even after controlling for past earnings. Communication between subjects increases the likelihood of cooperation (high prices) but does not significantly increase the use of harsh punishment. The findings suggest that in repeated games with rich action spaces, softer punishment strategies are more effective for sustaining cooperation and maximizing group payoffs.

This paper provides strong evidence that in repeated games with a rich action space (such as price competition), enabling punishment does not require harsh, maximal punishment to achieve high efficiency. Instead, proportionate, graduated punishment (e.g., Tit-for-tat) is more effective for maximizing group payoffs. For prediction tasks, this suggests that the presence of a punishment mechanism will likely increase efficiency, but the effect depends on the nature of punishment strategies adopted. Communication further supports cooperation but does not necessarily increase the use of harsh punishment. The findings are most directly relevant to repeated duopoly/oligopoly settings, but the payoff-based results are informative for adjacent public-goods-like environments.

column1: The paper studies a repeated two-player prisoner's dilemma with endogenous punishment: players can voluntarily make themselves vulnerable to punishment by allowing the partner to punish them at a cost. Two mechanisms are compared: 'Gradual' (vulnerability can be increased incrementally and conditionally) and 'Leap' (vulnerability is chosen in one simultaneous move). Both mechanisms significantly increase cooperation and efficiency compared to a control with no punishment, with the Gradual mechanism achieving the highest efficiency. Exogenously assigned punishment possibilities (no signaling) do not improve efficiency and can even reduce it due to inefficient punishment. The ability to signal willingness to cooperate by making oneself vulnerable is essential for the positive effect on efficiency.

Allowing players to endogenously make themselves vulnerable to punishment (i.e., to enable the partner to punish them at a cost) increases cooperation and efficiency in a repeated prisoner's dilemma compared to a control with no punishment. The Gradual mechanism, where vulnerability can be increased stepwise and conditionally, leads to higher mutual cooperation and efficiency than the Leap mechanism, where vulnerability is chosen in one step. column1: The paper studies repeated two-player prisoner's dilemma games with imperfect public monitoring, focusing on the effect of introducing a unilateral termination (dissolution) option as a punishment mechanism. The value and distribution of the outside option (termination payoff) are systematically varied. The presence of a termination option generally increases cooperation and efficiency when the outside option is low (termination is costly), but as the outside option increases above a threshold, efficiency drops sharply due to increased use of termination, which is inefficient. Further increases in the outside option then increase efficiency again, as the cost of termination falls. Asymmetric division rules for termination payoffs have large effects: rewarding the terminating party leads to almost universal early dissolution and very low efficiency, while rewarding the more cooperative party (arbitrator/judge rule) leads to very high cooperation and efficiency.

Introducing a termination (walk-away) option in repeated PD games increases cooperation and efficiency when the outside option is low, as termination is rarely used and serves as a credible threat. However, as the outside option rises above the in-relationship minmax, subjects begin to use termination more frequently as a punishment, leading to a sharp drop in efficiency. If the outside option increases further, efficiency rises again, as the cost of termination is less severe. Asymmetric division rules for termination payoffs have dramatic effects: if the party who terminates gets the higher payoff, almost all relationships dissolve immediately, resulting in very low efficiency. If the more cooperative party is rewarded, cooperation and efficiency are maximized. The paper provides direct evidence on how the structure and value of punishment options (termination) affect efficiency in repeated social dilemmas.

This paper provides strong evidence that the effect of punishment (here, the option to terminate a relationship) on efficiency is highly sensitive to the value and distribution of the punishment's payoff. When punishment is costly (low outside option), its mere availability increases efficiency, but if it becomes too attractive (high outside option), it is overused and efficiency drops. The design dimensions most relevant for prediction are the presence and value of the punishment option, the symmetry/asymmetry of its payoff, and the underlying game structure (here, repeated PD with imperfect monitoring). The findings suggest that the efficiency impact of enabling punishment depends non-monotonically on the cost/benefit of punishment, and that institutional details (who gets what on punishment/termination) can have very large effects. For prediction, the control efficiency (without punishment) and the specific design of the punishment option are critical moderators.

column1: This paper experimentally tests the Galbraith Mechanism (GM), a two-stage voluntary contribution game with heterogeneous endowments, where players allocate the public good among each other after observing contributions. The GM is compared to a standard equal-sharing control. The GM significantly increases efficiency (average group contributions and payoffs) and reduces inequality compared to the control, across a range of parameterizations. The effect is strongest when the marginal per-capita return (beta) is high enough. The mechanism does not involve costly punishment or reward, but the allocation stage allows for endogenous redistribution based on observed contributions.

The Galbraith Mechanism (GM) leads to higher efficiency (measured by average group contributions and payoffs) and lower inequality (measured by Gini coefficients) than the standard equal-sharing mechanism in voluntary contribution games with heterogeneous endowments. The GM's effect is robust across different levels of endowment inequality and marginal per-capita return (beta), though the effect is stronger when beta is higher. The mechanism works by allowing players to allocate the public good among each other based on observed contributions, incentivizing higher contributions without explicit punishment or reward costs. The GM outperforms the control in both efficiency and equity, especially benefiting the less-endowed players.

This paper provides strong evidence that mechanisms allowing endogenous allocation of the public good based on observed contributions (like the GM) can substantially increase efficiency compared to equal-sharing controls, even in the absence of explicit costly punishment or reward. For prediction tasks, the findings suggest that introducing a mechanism where players can allocate payoffs based on contributions (even without explicit punishment) can yield efficiency gains similar to or greater than those seen with standard punishment mechanisms, especially when the marginal per-capita return is sufficiently high. The results are most directly relevant for games with 3 players, 15 rounds, no chat, continuous contributions, and full information about others' contributions and allocations. The GM is not a punishment mechanism per se, but its allocation stage can serve a similar incentive function. The paper does not test standard punishment (costly reduction of others' payoffs), so direct quantitative transfer to punishment-enabled PGGs should be cautious, but the qualitative lesson is that endogenous, contribution-based allocation can strongly boost efficiency.

column1: Introducing punishment in this one-shot, two-player prisoner's dilemma reduces average payoffs (efficiency) compared to baseline. Social image concerns (being observed by a local authority) increase both cooperation and efficiency, but punishment—either alone or combined with social image—yields lower payoffs than baseline. Thus, punishment is detrimental to efficiency in this context.

The study finds that in a one-shot, two-player prisoner's dilemma, the presence of a local authority (Big Man) as an observer increases cooperation and leads to the highest average payoffs, exceeding baseline. Introducing a costly punishment stage (where players can spend to reduce the other's payoff) does not increase cooperation above the social image condition and results in lower average payoffs than baseline, due to the costs incurred by both punisher and punished. When both social image and punishment are present, efficiency is still lower than with social image alone and remains below baseline. The presence of an external (outgroup) authority does not increase cooperation or payoffs. Thus, punishment is not an efficient mechanism for promoting cooperation in this setting, and social image concerns are more effective.

This paper provides strong evidence that, in a one-shot, two-player PD with costly punishment, enabling punishment reduces efficiency compared to baseline (no punishment). The effect is robust: both punishment alone and punishment combined with social image concerns yield lower payoffs than baseline. The design is not a standard public goods game but is closely related (two-player PD with all-or-nothing contribution). The findings suggest that, for similar game designs (one-shot, small group, all-or-nothing, high punishment cost), enabling punishment is likely to reduce efficiency, even if it increases cooperation rates. The control (baseline) efficiency is higher than the punishment treatment efficiency. This evidence should be weighted heavily when predicting the effect of punishment in similar environments.

column1: The paper finds that enabling punishment (audits with fines) in a repeated capital budgeting game reduces slack and increases the superior's payoff (i.e., increases efficiency) when players are randomly rematched each round, regardless of reputation information. However, when the same pairs interact repeatedly (fixed matching), enabling punishment does not improve efficiency: slack increases and the superior's payoff decreases compared to the random matching case, and even compared to the no-audit control. Thus, punishment is effective in one-shot or random-matching settings but can backfire in repeated dyads due to negative reciprocity.

Audits (punishment) reduce slack and increase the superior's payoff (efficiency) in all random matching treatments, regardless of whether reputation information is provided. In these settings, subordinates reduce misreporting to avoid punishment, and superiors' willingness to audit is responsive to subordinates' past behavior. However, in fixed matching (repeated dyads), enabling audits leads to higher slack and lower superior payoff than in the random matching case, and even compared to the no-audit control. This is attributed to negative reciprocity: subordinates retaliate against superiors who punish them by increasing slack in later rounds, making punishment inefficient in repeated relationships. The effect of punishment on efficiency is thus positive in random matching but negative or null in fixed matching.

This paper provides strong evidence that the effect of punishment on efficiency depends critically on the matching protocol: punishment increases efficiency (superior payoff, lower slack) in random matching (analogous to one-shot or stranger settings), but not in fixed matching (repeated dyads), where it can decrease efficiency due to retaliation. For prediction, the presence of repeated interaction with the same partner (fixed matching) is a key moderator: enabling punishment is likely to increase efficiency in random matching but may have no effect or even reduce efficiency in fixed matching. Other design dimensions (e.g., reputation information) have smaller or secondary effects. The control efficiency (no-punishment) baseline is necessary for quantifying the effect size, but the direction of the effect is strongly moderated by the matching structure.

column1: The paper systematically analyzes the impact of direct punishment, third-party punishment, and their combinations (with and without partner selection and reputation) on the emergence of cooperation and group efficiency in multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) populations playing the Iterated Prisoner's Dilemma. It finds that direct punishment, especially when just punishment is net-rewarding, increases group efficiency (total reward) compared to no punishment. Direct punishment with partner selection achieves the highest societal reward at convergence, even though third-party punishment achieves higher cooperation rates. The combination of direct and third-party punishment leads to the fastest and highest convergence to cooperation, but at the cost of lower efficiency due to increased punishment costs. The results are robust across a range of population sizes.

Direct punishment, when just punishment is net-rewarding, is effective at promoting cooperation and maximizing group efficiency in MARL populations facing social dilemmas. Populations with direct punishment (especially with partner selection) achieve the highest total group reward at equilibrium, outperforming third-party punishment and combined punishment mechanisms in terms of efficiency, despite achieving slightly lower cooperation rates. Third-party punishment and combined punishment mechanisms lead to higher cooperation but incur greater punishment costs, reducing overall efficiency. The presence of partner selection and reputation further enhances the effectiveness of direct punishment. If just punishment is costly (i.e., not net-rewarding), neither cooperation nor punishment emerges, and group efficiency collapses. The findings are robust to changes in population size.

The results suggest that, for prediction tasks, the presence and type of punishment, the reward structure for just punishment, and the availability of partner selection and reputation are key moderators of the efficiency effect. The findings are directly relevant for predicting efficiency outcomes in adjacent social dilemma games (e.g., IPD) with similar design features, especially in artificial agent populations.

When the efficiency gain from larger groups is capped, groups remain smaller and less stable, and efficiency is lower, but still substantially higher than in fixed-group baselines. Redemption (the ability for excluded individuals to rejoin) further boosts efficiency. The results suggest that voluntary group formation with exclusion and merger mechanisms can solve the free-rider problem and achieve high efficiency in public goods provision.

column1: The paper finds that electoral delegation (democratic selection of a central allocator) in a public goods game leads to group outcomes that are close to the social optimum, with high efficiency and aggregate welfare. The results show that democratic delegation can overcome the free-rider problem and lead to efficient public goods provision.

The control efficiency (voluntary contribution) is very low in this design, but efficiency with delegation is near the social optimum. The results are most applicable to settings with large groups, low MPCR, and centralized decision-making via election.

column1: Across four lab experiments using a principal-agent game with subjective evaluation and costly punishment (conflict), the effect of enabling punishment on efficiency (total surplus) depends critically on the institutional context. In baseline, communication, and code-of-conduct (agreement) conditions, enabling punishment does not increase efficiency and often reduces it due to the direct costs of conflict outweighing small gains in effort. Only when punishment is institutionalized via a formal grievance procedure (grievance experiment) does enabling punishment lead to a significant increase in effort and a (statistically insignificant but positive) increase in total surplus, as norm coordination improves and conflicts become more targeted.

The paper finds that the effect of enabling punishment (conflict) in a principal-agent game with subjective evaluation is highly context-dependent. In the baseline, communication, and agreement (code of conduct) experiments, allowing workers to punish managers for not paying bonuses does not increase efficiency: the costs of conflict outweigh any small increases in effort, and total surplus is lower or unchanged compared to the no-punishment condition. Workers and managers fail to coordinate on an efficiency-enhancing norm, and punishment is often misapplied. However, when conflicts are institutionalized through a formal grievance process (grievance experiment), workers and managers coordinate more on a pay-for-output norm, effort increases significantly, and total surplus is higher in the punishment-enabled condition. Thus, punishment can enhance efficiency, but only when supported by strong institutional framing and norm coordination.

This paper provides strong evidence that the effect of enabling punishment on efficiency is not uniform and is highly sensitive to the institutional environment, especially the presence of mechanisms that coordinate norms (such as a grievance procedure). In environments lacking such coordination, enabling punishment is likely to reduce efficiency due to the direct costs of conflict. In contrast, when a formal grievance process is present, punishment can increase both effort and efficiency. For prediction tasks, the presence or absence of institutionalized conflict resolution and norm-coordination mechanisms should be considered a key moderator. Control efficiency (no-punishment) is not a reliable predictor of treatment efficiency (with punishment) unless the institutional context is specified.

column1: The paper experimentally demonstrates that institutionalized reciprocity (IR)—a mechanism where a reciprocal strategy is embedded as an institution—substantially increases group efficiency (total profit) in a repeated public goods game compared to a standard control condition. The effect is strongest when the institution restricts contributions to a target (S-IR), which prevents both free riding and excessive cooperation. The IR mechanism functions as a form of collective punishment: if any player fails to meet the target, the group's future maximum possible contribution (and thus profit) is reduced. This collective sanction is effective at sustaining high cooperation and efficiency, outperforming both the control and a less restrictive IR variant (NL-IR) where the target is only nominal.

In a repeated four-person public goods game, embedding a reciprocal strategy as an institution (institutionalized reciprocity, IR) leads to significantly higher group efficiency (total profit) than a standard control game. The effect is strongest when the institution enforces a strict upper bound on contributions (S-IR), which enables reciprocators to coordinate against free riders and prevents excessive cooperation. In S-IR, group profits are significantly higher than in both the control and a less restrictive IR variant (NL-IR). The IR mechanism operates as a collective punishment system: if any player fails to meet the target, the group's future benefit is reduced for all. The study does not implement standard peer punishment, but the IR mechanism provides a collective sanction that is effective at increasing efficiency.

While the study does not test standard peer punishment, it shows that collective, institutionally enforced sanctions can outperform standard repeated games without punishment. For prediction tasks, the findings suggest that introducing a credible, enforced institutional sanction (even if not peer punishment) can raise efficiency well above control, particularly when the rules are clear and binding. column1: This review synthesizes evidence from field studies and behavioral experiments on the governance of common-pool resources, emphasizing that institutional arrangements such as communication (cheap talk) and costly punishment can substantially increase group earnings and reduce overharvesting compared to baseline conditions without such mechanisms. The paper highlights that the effectiveness of interventions like punishment is context-dependent, influenced by group size, communication, trust, and broader social and ecological factors.

The paper finds that, contrary to the predictions of standard economic theory, groups can achieve higher efficiency and avoid the tragedy of the commons when allowed to communicate or implement costly punishment. Both lab and field experiments show that these mechanisms increase group earnings and reduce overuse of resources. The review also notes that centralized sanctioning mechanisms may be more effective and sustainable than peer punishment. However, the effectiveness of punishment and other interventions is context-specific, depending on factors such as group size, communication, trust, and cultural background. The paper also discusses the phenomenon of 'crowding out,' where externally imposed rules can sometimes reduce performance compared to voluntary agreements.

This paper supports the prediction that enabling punishment in public-goods-game-like environments generally increases group efficiency or earnings, especially when compared to baseline games without punishment or communication. It also highlights that the effect of punishment is moderated by contextual factors such as group size, communication, and the nature of the sanctioning institution (peer vs. centralized). While the review does not provide quantitative estimates, it offers strong qualitative evidence that punishment mechanisms, when available, tend to improve efficiency outcomes, but the magnitude and sustainability of these effects depend on the specific game design and social context.

column1: The paper shows that introducing the option for a first mover to act through an intermediary in a dictator-like game with third-party punishment reduces the amount of punishment imposed for selfish actions, even when the intermediary is completely passive and blameless. This reduction in punishment leads to much worse outcomes for the poorest player (the receiver) and lower group efficiency/surplus. The presence of an intermediary undermines the effectiveness of punishment as a tool for sustaining pro-social behavior, resulting in lower receiver payoffs and lower total group earnings.

The main finding is that when a first mover can choose to act selfishly either directly or via an intermediary, third-party punishment for selfishness is significantly lower when the action is taken through the intermediary. This is true even when the intermediary is passive and cannot be blamed. As a result, the poorest player (receiver) earns much less on average (from $4.50 to $1.63), and group earnings fall (from $19.55 to $17.24) when intermediation is available. The effect is robust to various controls and alternative explanations (e.g., diffusion of responsibility, confusion, lack of reasoning, or mere presence of a third party). The reduction in punishment is not explained by standard models of fairness or responsibility diffusion. The paper also finds that even when subjects are aware that intermediation is used to avoid punishment and that it harms the poorest player, they still punish less. A follow-up study shows a similar effect for rewards: indirect charitable giving is rewarded less than direct giving.

This paper provides strong evidence that the availability of an intermediary (a form of indirectness) in a punishment-enabled environment can dramatically reduce the effectiveness of punishment in sustaining pro-social outcomes, leading to lower efficiency and welfare. For prediction tasks, this suggests that game designs allowing for indirect actions or intermediation—even with punishment enabled—will likely see much lower efficiency than comparable direct-action games. The control (no intermediary) game with punishment achieves high receiver payoffs and group efficiency, but adding the intermediation option sharply reduces both, even though punishment is still available and costless. Thus, the presence of intermediation is a strong negative moderator of punishment's positive effect on efficiency.

column1: Introducing hierarchy into a linear public good game—by appointing an allocator (who determines all contributions) and further by allowing a principal to select the allocator—substantially increases group production and average incomes compared to the standard voluntary contribution mechanism. The study does not include explicit punishment or sanctioning mechanisms, but interprets voting as a safeguard against exploitation.

The study provides direct evidence on how institutional design (voting rules) affects efficiency in public good games, but does not test punishment or sanctioning per se.

column1: This theoretical paper analyzes a collective-risk social dilemma game (a variant of the public goods game with risk of group failure) using evolutionary game theory. It compares the effects of pure punishment, pure reward, and hybrid institutional incentive schemes (executors who both punish defectors and reward cooperators) on the prevalence of cooperation and group achievement. The main finding is that pure reward strategies outperform pure punishment and hybrid strategies in promoting group achievement (fraction of groups reaching the target), both under fixed and flexible institutional incentive schemes, and across a range of risk, mutation, and enhancement factor parameters. The paper does not report efficiency or total group payoff, but focuses on behavioral and institutional outcomes.

The paper finds that in collective-risk social dilemma games, institutional pure reward strategies (where executors only reward cooperators) are more effective than pure punishment or hybrid strategies in promoting group achievement (i.e., the fraction of groups that reach the collective target). This result holds for both fixed and flexible incentive schemes, and is robust to changes in risk level, mutation rate, and enhancement factor. Local sanctioning schemes are more effective than global ones. The main outcome is group achievement, not efficiency or total group payoff, so direct prediction of efficiency effects is not possible from this paper.

This paper provides indirect evidence relevant to predicting the effect of punishment on efficiency in public-goods-like games. It suggests that, in collective-risk social dilemmas, institutional punishment alone is less effective than reward or hybrid schemes in promoting group achievement (a proxy for cooperation). However, because the main outcome is not efficiency or group payoff, but rather the fraction of groups reaching a behavioral target, the findings should be used with caution for efficiency prediction. The game structure (collective-risk, institutional incentives, evolutionary dynamics) is close but not identical to standard PGGs. The results suggest that institutional punishment may not increase efficiency as much as reward, but do not provide quantitative efficiency estimates.

column1: This theoretical paper analyzes multiplayer evolutionary snowdrift games with collective punishment and reward mechanisms, focusing on how these mechanisms affect the frequency and stability of cooperation. The results show that collective punishment is more effective than collective reward in promoting and stabilizing high levels of cooperation, especially in small groups or when the initial frequency of cooperation is high. For large groups, collective punishment can still sustain full cooperation, while collective reward cannot. The main outcomes are the frequency of cooperation and the stability of cooperative equilibria, which are closely related to group payoff but not direct measures of efficiency.

The paper finds that collective punishment is more effective than collective reward in promoting and stabilizing cooperation in multiplayer snowdrift games, especially for small groups or high initial cooperation. When the punishment-to-benefit ratio exceeds a threshold, a stable state of full cooperation emerges for both small and large groups, while such a state does not appear for large groups with only reward. The main outcome is the frequency of cooperation, which is closely related to group payoff but not a direct measure of efficiency. The results suggest that, in environments where individual-level discrimination is not possible, collective punishment can maintain high cooperation and thus higher group fitness or payoff.

This paper provides strong theoretical support that, in multiplayer public-goods-like environments (specifically, snowdrift games), enabling collective punishment (even when it cannot be targeted at individuals) can substantially increase the frequency and stability of cooperation, especially in small groups or when the punishment intensity is high. This implies that, for prediction tasks, the presence and strength of collective punishment should be expected to increase efficiency or group payoff, particularly in small groups. However, the paper does not provide direct quantitative predictions of efficiency as defined by total group payoff relative to full cooperation, so the findings should be interpreted as indicating a strong positive effect on efficiency-related outcomes via increased cooperation rates and stable cooperative equilibria.

column1: This is a theoretical paper analyzing the effects of collective punishment (CP) in two classes of threshold public good games: (1) where resistance is individually costly but can produce a public good (CPG, e.g., protests), and (2) where resistance is individually profitable but produces a public bad (CPB, e.g., pollution). The main result is that in CPG games, the threat or application of CP never increases compliance (never reduces resistance), and may even backfire. In CPB games, CP can sometimes increase compliance, but only under certain parameter conditions (notably, when the individual gain from misbehavior is small relative to the social cost). The analysis is entirely theoretical, focusing on equilibrium selection and the probability of resistance, not on efficiency or group payoff as an explicit outcome.

The paper finds that collective punishment (CP) is ineffective or counterproductive in threshold public good games where resistance is individually costly but can produce a public good (e.g., protests, strikes). In these cases, increasing the threat or severity of CP does not increase compliance and may even increase resistance. In contrast, in threshold public bad games (e.g., pollution, crime), CP can sometimes increase compliance, but only when the individual benefit from misbehavior is small compared to the social cost. The paper provides formal equilibrium analysis and discusses equilibrium selection, but does not report efficiency or group payoff outcomes. The findings are relevant for predicting the behavioral effects of punishment in public-goods-like environments, especially regarding when punishment is likely to deter undesirable behavior.

This paper provides theoretical guidance on when collective punishment is likely to be effective in public-goods-like games. It suggests that in threshold public good games (where cooperation is costly and produces a group benefit), punishment is unlikely to increase efficiency or compliance, and may even be counterproductive. In threshold public bad games (where defection is individually profitable but socially costly), punishment can increase compliance and, by implication, efficiency, but only when the individual incentive to defect is not too large. The paper does not provide quantitative predictions for efficiency, but its qualitative results can inform predictions about the likely direction of punishment effects given the structure of the game (public good vs. public bad, cost/benefit ratios). However, because the paper does not analyze efficiency or group payoff directly, its support for efficiency prediction is indirect and should be supplemented with empirical or simulation evidence.

column1: This paper presents an agent-based evolutionary game model of trust in the sharing economy, where a dynamic reputation-based reward and punishment mechanism is implemented. The model shows that, compared to a baseline without reward/punishment, introducing reputation-based sanctions (punishment for low reputation, reward for high reputation) can increase the proportion of trustworthy participants and, with appropriate parameter settings, increase total group revenue (efficiency). However, excessively high punishment (high reputation threshold) can reduce total revenue, so there is an optimal intermediate threshold. The model is not a standard public goods game but is closely related, and the main outcome is total revenue, which is a direct efficiency measure.

The paper finds that implementing a dynamic, reputation-based reward and punishment mechanism in a trust game on a square lattice network increases the proportion of trustworthy participants and can increase total group revenue (efficiency) compared to a baseline without such mechanisms. The effect depends on the reputation threshold: moderate thresholds maximize both trust and total revenue, while very high thresholds reduce revenue due to excessive punishment. The model demonstrates that, for a wide range of initial conditions, appropriate punishment/reward settings can drive the system to full trust and higher efficiency. The results are robust to population size. The model is not a standard PGG but is adjacent, and the efficiency outcome is directly comparable.

This paper provides strong theoretical evidence that, in networked trust games with dynamic reputation-based punishment and reward, enabling punishment (and reward) can increase group efficiency compared to a baseline with no sanctions, provided the punishment/reward parameters are set appropriately. The effect is non-monotonic: too much punishment (high threshold) reduces efficiency, while moderate levels maximize it. For prediction tasks, this suggests that the presence and calibration of punishment/reward mechanisms are critical moderators of efficiency gains from sanctions. The model is adjacent to PGGs but the efficiency outcome is directly relevant.

column1: This theoretical paper analyzes how different punishment and dispute resolution schemes in repeated prisoner's dilemma games (with noise/unintentional noncompliance) affect the long-run efficiency (treaty value) for the group. It compares probabilistic trigger schemes (where both parties are punished after a deviation) to contrite tit-for-tat (CTFT) schemes with redress (where only the guilty party is punished and the victim is compensated). The main finding is that CTFT-type schemes, which combine generosity (delayed retaliation) and redress (compensation to the victim), yield higher long-run efficiency than trigger schemes, except in a narrow parameter range. The costliness of punishment to the punisher is a key determinant of efficiency loss under trigger schemes. The analysis is theoretical and does not present new empirical or experimental data.

The paper finds that in repeated prisoner's dilemma environments with possible unintentional noncompliance (noise), the design of punishment schemes has a large effect on long-run efficiency (treaty value). Probabilistic trigger schemes, which are analogous to mutual punishment phases after a deviation, are self-punishing and reduce efficiency because both the perpetrator and the victim suffer during punishment. Contrite tit-for-tat (CTFT) schemes, which allow for redress (compensation to the victim) and delay retaliation (generosity), achieve much higher efficiency by minimizing the time spent in mutual defection and ensuring that only the guilty party is punished. The paper provides explicit formulas and comparative statics for how efficiency declines with noise under each scheme, and shows that CTFT dominates trigger schemes in most of the relevant parameter space.

For the downstream prediction task, this paper provides strong theoretical evidence that the structure of the punishment scheme (especially whether punishment is self-punishing or allows for redress) is a critical moderator of the efficiency impact of punishment in repeated social dilemma games. If the punishment mechanism is costly to the punisher and involves mutual punishment phases (as in standard trigger schemes), efficiency is substantially reduced, especially as noise increases. If the punishment mechanism allows for redress (compensation to the victim) and avoids mutual punishment (as in CTFT), efficiency is much higher. The paper also shows that the speed of retaliation (trigger probability) and the expected duration of punishment phases are important: swifter, shorter punishments are more efficient, but only if they still deter defection. These insights should inform predictions about the efficiency effects of punishment based on the punishment technology, cost structure, and whether redress is possible.

column1: This paper presents an evolutionary game-theoretic model of a repeated public goods game with rewards (not punishment) on a dynamic network. The model shows that, under certain conditions (notably, when rewards are given only to contributors and network evolution is fast relative to strategy updating), high levels of public good provision and group efficiency can emerge endogenously. If rewards are also given to defectors, or if strategy updating is too fast, efficiency and public good provision are low. The model does not include punishment as a treatment, but discusses the role of exclusion (via network structure) as an endogenous sanctioning mechanism. The main outcomes are average group payoff and the efficiency of public good provision.

The model demonstrates that in a repeated public goods game with rewards (where giving rewards is costly but beneficial to the receiver), the emergence of a social institution prescribing prosocial behavior (contribute and reward contributors) can lead to efficient public good provision, provided that rewards are only given to contributors and the network structure evolves quickly enough to allow exclusion of non-contributors. If rewards are also given to defectors, or if players update strategies too quickly, the system converges to low contribution and low efficiency. The model does not analyze punishment directly, but exclusion from rewards via network dynamics acts as an endogenous sanction. The findings are theoretical and simulation-based, not empirical.

This paper is directly relevant for predicting efficiency in public goods games with reward mechanisms, especially in dynamic network settings. It provides strong theoretical evidence that reward-based institutions can achieve high efficiency if rewards are targeted only at contributors and if the network allows for exclusion of non-contributors. However, it does not provide evidence on the effect of punishment, nor does it compare reward to punishment directly. For prediction tasks focused on punishment-enabled vs. punishment-disabled games, this paper is only indirectly informative: it suggests that endogenous exclusion (a form of sanction) can substitute for explicit punishment, but does not quantify the effect of punishment per se. The model's results are most applicable to games with dynamic partner selection and reward, not to standard fixed-group punishment treatments.

column1: This theoretical paper analyzes how different punishment strategies and information transmission regimes affect the sustainability and efficiency of cooperation in networks of repeated Prisoner's Dilemma games. It shows that allowing for word-of-mouth communication and using forgiving (repentance) punishment strategies increases the set of conditions (discount factors) under which cooperation (and thus efficiency) can be sustained, compared to unforgiving (grim trigger/contagion) strategies. The paper provides explicit equilibrium conditions for when cooperation is sustainable and demonstrates that more efficient outcomes are possible with communication and targeted punishment.

The paper finds that in networks of repeated Prisoner's Dilemma games, the ability to transmit information (word-of-mouth) and the use of forgiving, targeted punishment strategies (Multilateral Repentance) allow for cooperation to be sustained under a wider range of conditions (i.e., lower discount factors) than under traditional contagion (Grim Trigger) strategies. This leads to higher efficiency and welfare, especially during punishment phases, as only defectors are punished and cooperation among others continues. The structure of the network (closure, density) and the speed of information transmission further moderate these effects. The results are formalized in terms of equilibrium payoff conditions and sustainability criteria.

For the prediction task, this paper provides strong theoretical evidence that enabling targeted, forgiving punishment (as opposed to all-or-nothing breakdowns) and facilitating information transmission (communication) in networked repeated social dilemmas increases the efficiency of cooperation. The results suggest that, all else equal, punishment regimes that are more targeted and allow for communication will yield higher efficiency than those that rely on contagious, permanent breakdowns. The paper also highlights the importance of network structure (closure, density) and information speed, which may inform how design dimensions like communication, punishment technology, and information feedback affect efficiency. However, the results are theoretical and do not provide quantitative effect sizes.

column1: The paper provides a theoretical analysis of a generalized volunteer's dilemma (VD) in which more than one volunteer is required to prevent a social harm, and participation costs are private information. It compares the efficiency of outcome-based, action-based, and combined punishment/reward policies for inducing socially optimal participation. The main result is that action-based (and some combined) policies can uniquely induce the efficient (second-best) outcome and rule out the inefficient no-participation equilibrium, while outcome-based policies always allow for a no-participation equilibrium when more than one volunteer is needed. Action-based policies also require lower total payments (punishments/rewards) than outcome-based policies to achieve the same efficiency.

Theoretical analysis shows that action-based punishment/reward policies are superior to outcome-based policies in generalized volunteer's dilemma settings (where more than one volunteer is needed and costs are private). Action-based policies can uniquely induce the efficient (second-best) outcome and prevent the no-participation equilibrium, while outcome-based policies always allow for a no-participation equilibrium, which is stable and potentially focal. The required level of punishment/reward under action-based policies is lower than under outcome-based policies. Combined policies that include punishment for non-participation can also rule out the no-participation equilibrium. The analysis is grounded in social cost minimization and group welfare, not just participation rates.

This paper provides strong theoretical support for the prediction that punishment (when implemented as action-based or combined with action-contingency) will have a more positive effect on efficiency (group welfare, social cost minimization) than outcome-based punishment in public-goods-like environments where more than one participant is needed. The results suggest that the design of the punishment mechanism (action-based vs. outcome-based) is a critical moderator: action-based punishment can uniquely induce efficient outcomes and prevent social traps, while outcome-based punishment may fail to improve efficiency if the no-participation equilibrium is selected. The findings are directly relevant for predicting the effect of punishment on efficiency, especially in settings with binary (all-or-nothing) participation, private costs, and no coordination. However, the results are theoretical and based on a generalized volunteer's dilemma, which is adjacent but not identical to standard PGGs.

column1: This paper develops an evolutionary game-theoretic model in which specialized third-party enforcers can sustain cooperation among producers via costly punishment, even when direct and indirect reciprocity are ineffective. The model shows that, under certain parameter conditions, the presence of third-party punishment leads to a cooperative equilibrium with higher average payoffs (efficiency) for both producers and enforcers, compared to a defection equilibrium without punishment. The effect of punishment on efficiency is strongly moderated by the costs and effectiveness of enforcement, the destructiveness of enforcer conflict, and the severity of punishment.

The model demonstrates that specialized third-party punishment can enable and sustain high-efficiency cooperative equilibria in social dilemmas where direct and indirect reciprocity fail. When enforcers are incentivized (via reputation and meta-enforcement) to punish defectors, producers cooperate, and both groups achieve higher payoffs. The efficiency gain from punishment depends on the cost and effectiveness of punishment, the cost of information, and the destructiveness of enforcer conflict. If punishment is too costly or weak, or if enforcer conflict is not destructive enough, the system collapses to a low-efficiency defection equilibrium. The model also shows that the cooperative equilibrium is robust to the presence of alternative (non-cooperation-enforcing) reputation systems, but only if the key parameter thresholds are met.

This paper provides strong theoretical evidence that enabling punishment by specialized third-party enforcers can substantially increase efficiency in public-goods-like environments, but only if the punishment is sufficiently severe, not too costly, and enforcers are themselves disciplined (e.g., via meta-enforcement and reputation). The model clarifies which game design dimensions (punishment cost, punishment effectiveness, information cost, severity of punishment, and the structure of enforcement interactions) are critical moderators of the efficiency effect. For prediction, the presence of third-party punishment should be expected to increase efficiency relative to a no-punishment baseline, provided the relevant costs and incentives are favorable. However, if punishment is weak, costly, or undisciplined, efficiency gains may not materialize.

For institutional incentives, both punishment and reward can achieve similar cooperation levels, but reward produces positive social welfare over a much wider range of parameters. Increasing the impact or efficiency of punishment does not necessarily improve social welfare and can be detrimental. The objectives of maximizing cooperation and maximizing social welfare are often misaligned.

The paper finds that in evolutionary models of the Prisoner's Dilemma with peer or institutional incentives, punishment mechanisms (both peer and institutional) are often detrimental to social welfare, even when they increase cooperation. Peer punishment increases cooperation more than peer reward, but peer reward leads to higher social welfare. For institutional incentives, reward achieves positive social welfare across a broader range of parameters than punishment, even when both achieve similar cooperation levels. There is often an optimal, moderate level of incentive impact for maximizing social welfare, rather than maximizing cooperation or punishment strength. These findings are robust across mutation rates, selection intensities, and game configurations.

For prediction tasks, the presence of punishment (especially with high impact-to-cost ratio) should be expected to have a less positive or even negative effect on efficiency relative to control, unless the punishment is extremely cost-effective and moderate in impact. In maximally connected cliques, punishment is most effective due to perfect monitoring, and full cooperation (and thus maximal efficiency) is sustainable if all individuals are sufficiently patient. However, when some individuals are impatient (low discount factor), cliques can lead to cascades of defection and lower welfare. In such cases, less connected networks (e.g., grids) can isolate the effects of uncooperative types, allowing more tolerant individuals to absorb free riding and maintain higher overall welfare. The optimal network design thus balances the benefits of effective punishment (which requires connectivity and observability) against the costs of social conflict from connecting intolerant and uncooperative types. The paper provides explicit formulas for expected welfare under different network designs and type distributions.

It shows that punishment is most effective (and efficiency is highest) in small, maximally connected groups with perfect monitoring and homogeneous patience. As heterogeneity increases, or as monitoring becomes more local/imperfect, the efficiency gains from punishment can be reduced or even reversed, with less connected networks sometimes yielding higher welfare. column1: This theoretical paper shows that in large-population, randomly-matched repeated prisoner's dilemma games with anonymous players and no identification or communication, cooperation can be sustained in equilibrium through 'contagious' punishment strategies. These strategies can support nearly efficient outcomes (i.e., payoffs close to full cooperation) for sufficiently patient players, even in the presence of small amounts of noise (mistakes). The results are robust to the absence of public randomization devices and to some heterogeneity in discount factors. The efficiency of the cooperative equilibrium approaches the fully cooperative level as the probability of mistakes goes to zero and as players become more patient.

The paper demonstrates that contagious punishment strategies can sustain cooperation and near-efficient payoffs in large, anonymous, randomly-matched repeated prisoner's dilemma games. The equilibrium is robust to small amounts of noise (players making mistakes) and does not require excessive patience except in very large populations or when the gain from defection is very small. The efficiency loss due to noise can be made arbitrarily small as the noise probability decreases. The results hold even without public randomization devices, though the required patience may increase in some parameter regimes. The analysis provides explicit conditions (in terms of discount factor, population size, and gain from defection) under which efficient cooperation is possible.

The results are most directly applicable to repeated prisoner's dilemma games, which are adjacent to public goods games. column1: This theoretical paper analyzes how informal punishment and reward schemes, determined by a principal's social preferences rather than ex ante contracts, affect efficiency and surplus in environments with externalities. It distinguishes between 'intent-based justice' (punishment only with sufficient belief in guilt) and 'outcome-based justice' (punishment based on outcomes regardless of intent). The model shows that intent-based justice can approach efficient outcomes as monitoring becomes perfect, but may also admit inefficient equilibria, especially with positive externalities. Outcome-based justice guarantees a minimum share of the efficient surplus but is always bounded away from first-best efficiency due to transfer costs and lack of use of side information. The model is adjacent to public goods games, focusing on a principal-agent setting with externalities rather than a symmetric multi-player PGG.

The paper finds that informal punishment and reward schemes, when based on social preferences and ex post moral judgment, can partially or fully internalize externalities and improve efficiency, but the effect depends on the type of justice (intent-based vs. outcome-based), the quality of information, and the nature of the externality (positive or negative). Intent-based justice can achieve high efficiency with good monitoring but is less robust and can result in multiple equilibria, including inefficient ones. Outcome-based justice is more robust but less efficient, as it does not exploit side information and always incurs transfer costs. The model provides explicit formulas for the efficiency loss under each regime and characterizes when punishment will or will not be used.

column1: This theoretical paper analyzes the coevolution of altruism and punishment in a two-player game with four strategies (altruist punisher, altruist non-punisher, selfish punisher, selfish non-punisher), under both well-mixed and lattice-structured populations, and under two evolutionary update rules (score-dependent viability and fertility). The main findings are that punishment can promote the evolution of cooperation (and thus higher group payoffs) under some conditions, especially when the cost of being punished is high relative to the cost of punishing, and in spatially structured populations. However, the effect depends strongly on the model details: in some cases, punishment does not invade or even hinders cooperation, and the presence of 'selfish punishers' can paradoxically help or hinder cooperation depending on context. The paper does not report explicit efficiency or group payoff values, but the prevalence of cooperative strategies is used as a proxy.

The paper finds that punishment can promote the evolution of cooperation (and thus higher group payoffs) in both well-mixed and lattice-structured populations, but only under certain conditions. In the score-dependent viability model, punishment is more effective at suppressing defectors and promoting cooperation than in the fertility model. The presence of selfish punishers (defectors who punish other defectors) can help the evolution of altruistic punishers by first eliminating pure defectors, but pure altruists (who cooperate but do not punish) can hinder the evolution of punishment by being exploited. The benefit of cooperation, the fine imposed by punishment, and the cost of punishing all interact to determine evolutionary outcomes. The effect of punishment on efficiency is thus context-dependent and can be positive or negative depending on parameter values and population structure.

This paper provides theoretical evidence that the effect of punishment on efficiency (group payoff) in public-goods-like games depends on the interaction of several design dimensions: population structure (well-mixed vs. lattice), the cost and effectiveness of punishment, the benefit of cooperation, and the evolutionary update rule (viability vs. fertility). Punishment is more likely to increase efficiency when the punishment fine is large relative to the cost of punishing, and in spatially structured populations. However, if the cost of punishing is too high or if pure cooperators are common, punishment may not evolve or may even reduce cooperation. The findings suggest that predictions of treatment efficiency from control efficiency should account for these moderators, especially the structure of interactions and the punishment parameters. However, as the paper does not report explicit efficiency values, its support is indirect and based on evolutionary stability of cooperation.
